scenarios.title: Whose patch is it?
scenarios.situation: A VM running in a public cloud IaaS account is breached through an unpatched operating system. The customer argues the cloud provider should have patched it.
scenarios.prompt: Who is responsible for patching the guest OS under the shared-responsibility model?
choices: The customer — in IaaS the provider secures the physical layer and hypervisor; the guest OS is yours
The cloud provider — they own everything below your data
Nobody — shared means neither side
The OS vendor, automatically
scenarios.why: Shared responsibility splits at the hypervisor for IaaS: the provider secures facilities, hardware, and virtualization; you own the OS, middleware, apps, and data. The line moves up the stack with PaaS and SaaS, but IaaS guests are always the customer's job.
scenarios.hint: In IaaS, where does the provider's job end?

scenarios.title: The spiky web app
scenarios.situation: An e-commerce app idles most of the day but gets 20x traffic spikes during flash sales. It currently runs on one oversized VM, 24/7.
scenarios.prompt: What architecture handles this most cost-effectively?
choices: A load balancer with auto-scaling: add instances as traffic rises, remove them as it falls
A single even bigger VM running all the time
Vertical scaling by hand before each sale
Move it back on-premises
scenarios.why: Auto-scaling matches capacity to demand automatically, and the load balancer spreads traffic across the fleet. Paying for peak capacity around the clock wastes money; manual vertical scaling is slow and error-prone under flash-sale pressure.
scenarios.hint: What matches capacity to demand without a human watching?

scenarios.title: Picking the storage tier
scenarios.situation: An app needs storage for two things: millions of user-uploaded images, and a relational database with heavy random reads and writes.
scenarios.prompt: Which pairing is correct?
choices: Object storage for the images; block storage volumes for the database
Block storage for everything
File storage for everything
Archive tape for the database
scenarios.why: Object storage is built for massive numbers of flat, immutable blobs (images, backups) with HTTP access; databases need low-latency block devices that look like local disks. Matching the access pattern to the storage type is a core Cloud+ skill.
scenarios.hint: What storage is built for billions of flat files?

scenarios.title: The deadline migration
scenarios.situation: A legacy app must leave a colo data center before the contract ends in three months. There is no time for a rewrite.
scenarios.prompt: Which migration strategy fits, and what is the trade-off?
choices: Lift-and-shift (rehost) now to meet the deadline, then plan modernization later — it carries tech debt into the cloud
Refactor to cloud-native first, deadline or not
Stay and renegotiate at any cost
Rewrite from scratch in three months
scenarios.why: Rehosting moves the app as-is: fastest, lowest risk to the deadline, but you inherit on-prem architectures (and costs) in the cloud. Refactoring is better long-term but cannot fit the timeline — so rehost now, replatform/refactor in phases.
scenarios.hint: What gets you moved before the contract ends?

scenarios.title: The residency requirement
scenarios.situation: A healthcare company wants cloud elasticity, but regulations require patient records to stay in-country in facilities it controls.
scenarios.prompt: Which deployment model fits?
choices: Hybrid cloud: regulated data on the private side, elastic workloads bursting to public
All-public cloud — regulations are just paperwork
All on-premises — give up elasticity
Ignore the residency rule
scenarios.why: Hybrid keeps sensitive data where the law demands while using public cloud for scale where it is allowed. Data residency and sovereignty requirements are hard constraints that architecture must satisfy, not risks to accept.
scenarios.hint: Where must regulated data physically live?

scenarios.title: The surprise bill
scenarios.situation: The monthly cloud bill doubled. Investigation shows dozens of idle dev VMs running 24/7 and untagged resources nobody claims.
scenarios.prompt: What is the systematic fix?
choices: Rightsizing, mandatory tagging with ownership, and auto-shutdown schedules for non-production
Pay the bill and hope next month is better
Buy a bigger discount plan and change nothing
Move to another cloud
scenarios.why: Cloud waste is an operational discipline problem: tagging establishes ownership for chargeback, rightsizing matches instances to actual use, and schedules kill idle dev spend. FinOps basics beat provider-hopping every time.
scenarios.hint: What identifies who owns each resource?

scenarios.title: Multi-Region Checkout Resilience
scenarios.situation: Your e-commerce checkout service runs in a single cloud region behind a load balancer. During a regional incident last month, checkout was down for 90 minutes and the postmortem blamed a single AZ dependency. Management now demands checkout stay up during any single-region failure, but the database team warns that splitting the order database across regions could corrupt orders.
scenarios.prompt: Which architecture keeps checkout available through a regional outage without risking order integrity?
choices: Active-passive with DNS failover and a synchronous multi-region relational database for orders
Active-active checkout front ends in two regions, region-local payment intake queues, and a single authoritative order ledger reconciled by idempotency keys
Replicate the full checkout stack into three regions with asynchronous eventual-consistency replication of the order database
Move checkout to a single larger region with three availability zones and double the instance count
scenarios.why: Payment intake can be parallelized per region (each queue holds durable, idempotent requests), while money movement requires exactly-one canonical ledger — idempotency keys let the single ledger absorb duplicate intake safely. Option A stalls on cross-region latency of synchronous commits and DNS failover is slow; C risks split-brain order state; D still dies with the region.
scenarios.hint: Ask which part of checkout tolerates parallelism and which part demands exactly-once.

scenarios.title: Burst Traffic on a Fixed Budget
scenarios.situation: A marketing site gets 200 visitors per hour normally, but TV ad spots drive 40x spikes for 20 minutes, three times a week. The current fleet is statically provisioned for peak and finance wants the idle spend cut by half. The app is stateless except for sessions stored on local disk.
scenarios.prompt: What combination handles the spikes and satisfies finance?
choices: Keep the peak fleet but convert half of it to spot instances
Auto-scaling group with target-tracking on request count, sessions moved to a shared session store, plus a CDN in front of static content
Scheduled scaling that doubles instances for the 20-minute ad windows
Containerize and run everything on a single large instance with burstable CPU
scenarios.why: Auto-scaling on a real demand metric matches capacity to the spike while sessions in a shared store let any instance serve any user (local-disk sessions break under scaling). A CDN absorbs the bulk of read traffic cheaply. Spot instances (A) get reclaimed exactly when ads air is not guaranteed and scheduled scaling (C) misses unscheduled spikes; a single box (D) is a failure domain.
scenarios.hint: What breaks first when instances come and go mid-session?
objectives: Separate stateless compute from session state

scenarios.title: The unreadable web files
scenarios.situation: After a restore, the web server returns 403 Forbidden on every page. The files are owned by the deploy user.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong and what is the fix?
choices: Files are 600 — the web server user cannot read them; set files to 644 and directories to 755
Set everything to 777 so nothing is ever blocked
Change ownership to root
Reinstall the web server
scenarios.why: 600 gives read/write to the owner only; the web server runs as a different user and needs read on files plus read+execute on directories to traverse them. 644/755 is the standard; 777 hands write access to everyone — a vulnerability, not a fix.
scenarios.hint: What does the web server user need — read, write, or both?

scenarios.title: The failed service
scenarios.situation: After a reboot, the application service did not start. The config file was edited yesterday.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct diagnostic sequence?
choices: systemctl status app.service, then journalctl -u app.service to read the failure logs
Reboot again and hope
Reinstall the application
kill -9 the service
scenarios.why: systemctl status shows the state and the most recent log lines; journalctl -u gives the full story, usually a config syntax error from yesterday's edit. Guessing with reinstalls wastes the evidence systemd already collected.
scenarios.hint: Where does systemd keep the service's last words?

scenarios.title: Root filesystem full
scenarios.situation: A Linux host alerts: the root filesystem is at 100%. The application data lives on a separate mounted volume with free space.
scenarios.prompt: How do you find and fix it?
choices: Use du to find the growth (often /var/log), then rotate, compress, or archive — never delete blindly
Run rm -rf /var to clear space fast
Add RAM
Reboot and hope the filesystem recovers
scenarios.why: df identifies the full filesystem, du -sh /* drills into the culprit — typically unrotated logs. Deleting system directories breaks the OS; logrotate plus archival fixes the cause and prevents recurrence.
scenarios.hint: Which command shows where the gigabytes actually are?

scenarios.title: The brute-force noise
scenarios.situation: Auth logs show thousands of SSH password attempts per hour against your public-facing Linux server.
scenarios.prompt: What is the strongest mitigation set?
choices: Key-only authentication (disable PasswordAuthentication), plus fail2ban and no direct root login
Just change the SSH port and call it done
Allow root login for convenience
Use longer passwords and keep password auth
scenarios.why: Keys cannot be guessed, so disabling password auth kills brute force entirely; fail2ban adds rate-limiting, and PermitRootLogin no stops the highest-value target. Changing ports is obscurity — it reduces log noise, not risk.
scenarios.hint: What authentication method cannot be guessed?

scenarios.title: The silent cron job
scenarios.situation: A backup script runs perfectly by hand but never runs from cron. There are no errors anywhere obvious.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
choices: Cron's minimal environment — missing PATH or env vars the script relied on from your shell
Cron is broken on this server
The server needs a reboot
Run it manually forever instead
scenarios.why: Cron runs with a sparse environment: no interactive PATH, no aliases, no sourced profiles. Scripts that assume your shell's environment fail silently. Fixes: absolute paths, explicit env vars in the crontab, and logging output to a file.
scenarios.hint: What environment does cron NOT give your script?

scenarios.title: Installing from the wild
scenarios.situation: A blog post says to install a monitoring agent with curl | sudo bash from the author's personal site.
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe alternative?
choices: Install from the official distro repository or the vendor's signed repo via apt/dnf, verifying signatures
Pipe the script — the blog has many likes
Download a random tarball and compile as root
Disable GPG checking to make installs faster
scenarios.why: curl|bash executes unaudited code as root from whoever controls that server today. Official repositories provide signed, versioned, updatable packages — the supply-chain-safe path. Convenience is not a security control.
scenarios.hint: Who signed that package — and who controls the download server?

scenarios.title: Web Service Won't Start After Reboot
scenarios.situation: After a kernel update and reboot, the company's nginx-based portal refuses to start. `systemctl status nginx` shows 'failed' and the journal mentions 'bind() to 0.0.0.0:443 failed (13: Permission denied)'. The config hasn't changed and the service ran fine before the reboot. SELinux is in enforcing mode.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause, and the correct first fix?
choices: The update wiped the SSL certificate; regenerate the cert and restart
A stale PID file survived the reboot; delete it and start the service
nginx is running as a non-root user via a changed systemd unit, or SELinux is blocking the port bind; check the unit's User= and audit logs with ausearch
Port 443 is already in use by another service; kill whatever holds it
scenarios.why: Permission denied on bind to a privileged port (<1024) means the process lacks the capability — either the systemd unit now drops privileges before binding, or SELinux denies the socket bind (check `ausearch -m avc -ts recent`). Certs (A) produce TLS errors, not bind errors; PID files (B) don't survive reboots meaningfully; another listener (D) gives 'address already in use', not permission denied.
scenarios.hint: Read the exact errno message — it says permission, not conflict.

scenarios.title: Disk Full But du Disagrees
scenarios.situation: Monitoring alerts that /var is 100% full on a database server, yet `du -sh /var/*` totals only 60% of the filesystem. The database is still writing and a junior admin suggests rebooting to 'clear it up'. Application logs are being written to /var/log/app at high volume.
scenarios.prompt: What explains the mismatch, and what is the safe fix?
choices: Filesystem corruption; run fsck on /var immediately
Deleted-but-still-open log files held by the app process; find them with lsof and have the app reopen logs (e.g., via logrotate copytruncate or SIGHUP)
Reserved blocks for root; lower the reserved percentage with tune2fs
Inode exhaustion; delete small files to free inodes
scenarios.why: When a file is deleted while a process holds it open, `du` can't see it but the space isn't freed — the classic df-vs-du gap. `lsof | grep deleted` finds the culprits; rotating with copytruncate or signaling the app to reopen logs releases the space without data loss. fsck (A) needs downtime and addresses corruption, not this; reserved blocks (C) show as unavailable in df, not a du gap; inodes (D) show 'no space left' with df space free.
scenarios.hint: The space is invisible to du but still allocated — who is holding it?
evidence: Uses lsof to find deleted open files

scenarios.title: Four disks, speed plus safety
scenarios.situation: A database server has four identical disks. Requirements: good performance AND survive at least one disk failure.
scenarios.prompt: Which RAID level is the best fit?
choices: RAID 10
RAID 0
RAID 5
JBOD
scenarios.why: RAID 10 is a stripe of mirrors: mirroring survives disk failures (and rebuilds fast), striping delivers performance. RAID 0 has no redundancy, and RAID 5's parity rebuilds on large disks are slow and risky — RAID 10 is the standard answer for performance + redundancy.
scenarios.hint: Which level is a stripe of mirrors?

scenarios.title: The random crashes
scenarios.situation: A server crashes randomly with no useful logs — sometimes kernel panics, sometimes application faults, never the same error twice.
scenarios.prompt: What hardware cause should you suspect, and what is server-grade prevention?
choices: Failing RAM / cosmic-bit flips — use ECC memory, which detects and corrects single-bit errors, and test the DIMMs
The OS needs reinstalling
The PSU is too big
Ignore it; random crashes are normal
scenarios.why: Inconsistent, unlogged crashes are the classic signature of memory errors. ECC RAM corrects single-bit errors in hardware and logs them — which is why servers use it and desktops usually do not. Memtest plus DIMM isolation finds the bad stick.
scenarios.hint: What flips bits silently with no log entry?

scenarios.title: The dead power supply
scenarios.situation: Monitoring alerts: one of two redundant PSUs has failed, but the server is still running.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct action?
choices: Hot-swap the failed PSU now — that is what redundancy is for — and verify the redundancy configuration
Power the server down first to be safe
Ignore it since the server is up
Replace both PSUs
scenarios.why: Redundant hot-swappable PSUs exist so a failure is a maintenance event, not an outage — but redundancy is now gone, so the next failure is fatal. Replace promptly during a planned moment, and confirm the PSUs are on separate circuits.
scenarios.hint: What is the second PSU for?

scenarios.title: The hot aisle
scenarios.situation: Temperature sensors show a steady climb in one rack row over two weeks. Servers there are thermal-throttling.
scenarios.prompt: What do you check first?
choices: Airflow and cooling: HVAC function, blanking panels, hot/cold aisle containment, blocked vents
Install more servers in the row
Open all the rack doors permanently
Ignore it until something shuts down
scenarios.why: Heat problems are airflow problems first: missing blanking panels let hot exhaust recirculate into intakes, defeating the HVAC. Hot/cold aisle discipline plus sealed racks keeps cooling effective; adding load or opening doors makes it worse.
scenarios.hint: Where does the hot exhaust air go?

scenarios.title: POST reports memory errors
scenarios.situation: A server fails to boot, and POST reports memory errors on DIMM B2.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct procedure?
choices: Reseat the DIMMs, then test one at a time to isolate the faulty stick and replace it
Update the BIOS and hope
Reinstall the OS
Ignore POST errors
scenarios.why: POST memory errors localize the fault to a slot or stick. Reseating fixes contact issues; single-stick testing isolates the failure; replace only the bad DIMM. Firmware updates do not fix bad RAM, and the OS is irrelevant before boot.
scenarios.hint: What is the cheapest test you can run first?

scenarios.title: The hung server 200 miles away
scenarios.situation: A branch-office server is completely hung — no SSH, no services. Driving there takes four hours.
scenarios.prompt: What capability resolves this remotely?
choices: Out-of-band management (BMC / iDRAC / iLO) for console access and power control independent of the OS
Wait for it to fix itself
Ask a non-technical employee to pull the plug
Reinstall the OS remotely
scenarios.why: Baseboard management controllers run independently of the host OS: they give KVM console, power cycle, and hardware sensors even when the OS is dead. It is the standard answer for lights-out remote sites — no BMC means a truck roll.
scenarios.hint: What manages the server when the OS is dead?

scenarios.title: RAID Choice for a Write-Heavy Database
scenarios.situation: You're speccing local storage for a write-heavy transactional database server with eight SSDs. The DBA demands both strong write performance and survival of a double-disk failure. The hardware RAID controller has a battery-backed cache. Budget allows any RAID level.
scenarios.prompt: Which RAID level best meets the requirements?
choices: RAID 5: striping with single parity, best usable capacity
RAID 6: striping with double parity, survives two disk failures
RAID 10: mirrored stripes, survives one failure per mirror pair
RAID 0: pure striping, maximum write throughput
scenarios.why: RAID 6 is the only option that both tolerates two simultaneous disk failures and keeps striping throughput. RAID 5 dies on a second failure during the long rebuild window; RAID 10 survives only if the second failure lands in a different mirror pair — the wrong pair fails and the array is gone; RAID 0 has no redundancy at all. The battery-backed cache mitigates RAID 6's write-parity penalty.
scenarios.hint: Which option guarantees survival when ANY two specific disks fail?
objectives: Select RAID levels for workload requirements

scenarios.title: Mysterious Throttling Under Load
scenarios.situation: A 2U application server performs fine for 10 minutes under load, then throughput collapses to 40% and stays there until idle for a while. CPU frequency monitoring shows the cores dropping to their minimum P-state during the collapse. Ambient datacenter temperature is normal and no alerts fire.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely hardware-level cause?
choices: A failing power supply dropping to redundant-half capacity
Thermal throttling: heatsink clogged or thermal paste degraded, so the CPU hits its thermal limit under sustained load
Bad RAM triggering ECC corrections that stall the pipeline
The RAID controller battery failing, forcing write-through mode
scenarios.why: The time-delayed onset plus recovery after idle is the signature of heat soak: the CPU runs full speed until the heatsink saturates, then firmware clamps frequency to protect the chip. PSU issues (A) would trip immediately or reboot; ECC errors (C) log correctable-error counters and don't follow a clean 10-minute curve; write-through cache (D) affects disk writes, not CPU P-states.
scenarios.hint: What physical process takes 10 minutes to build up and dissipates when idle?
evidence: Links P-state drop to heat soak

scenarios.title: Snapshots are not backups
scenarios.situation: An admin proudly reports the VMs are 'backed up' — they take a snapshot of each VM every night and keep them for a month.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this picture?
choices: Snapshots are not backups: they live on the same storage, grow into performance problems, and die with the datastore
Nothing — snapshots are a complete backup strategy
They should take more snapshots
They should delete old snapshots to save space and call it done
scenarios.why: A snapshot is a delta file chained to the base disk on the same storage: lose the datastore and you lose base plus snapshots. Long snapshot chains also degrade performance. Real backups are independent, restorable copies — ideally offsite and tested.
scenarios.hint: What happens to the snapshots when the datastore dies?

scenarios.title: The sluggish VMs
scenarios.situation: VMs on a host are sluggish though the host's CPU graphs look fine. The hypervisor reports high CPU ready time.
scenarios.prompt: What is the cause and fix?
choices: vCPU overprovisioning — VMs are waiting for physical CPU; right-size vCPUs and check contention
Give every VM more vCPUs
Add more RAM to the host
Reboot the host weekly
scenarios.why: CPU ready time measures how long a VM waits for a physical core: over-allocated vCPUs make scheduling harder, not faster. Adding vCPUs to contended hosts worsens it. Right-sizing plus DRS-style balancing restores performance.
scenarios.hint: What does CPU ready time actually measure?

scenarios.title: Fifty microservices
scenarios.situation: A team needs to run fifty small microservices that scale up and down frequently. Full VMs feel heavy and slow to start.
scenarios.prompt: Why are containers the better fit here?
choices: Containers share the host kernel, so they start in milliseconds with far less overhead than full VMs
Containers are just faster VMs with their own kernels
One VM per microservice is simpler
Bare metal for each service
scenarios.why: Containers package the app with its dependencies but share the host OS kernel — no guest OS per instance, no hypervisor boot. That means sub-second starts and dense packing, ideal for elastic microservices. VMs still win where strong isolation or different kernels are needed.
scenarios.hint: What do containers share that VMs do not?

scenarios.title: Patching without downtime
scenarios.situation: A hypervisor host needs firmware patches, but its twenty VMs cannot have downtime.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct procedure?
choices: Live-migrate (vMotion) the running VMs to another host, patch the empty host, then migrate back
Shut everything down for the patch window
Patch the host with VMs running on it
Skip the firmware patches
scenarios.why: Live migration moves running VMs between hosts with no downtime, letting you evacuate a host for maintenance. It requires shared storage and compatible hosts — the standard enterprise maintenance workflow.
scenarios.hint: What moves a running VM without stopping it?

scenarios.title: Choosing the hypervisor
scenarios.situation: You are designing a new virtualization cluster for production workloads needing near-native performance and strong isolation.
scenarios.prompt: Which hypervisor type fits, and why?
choices: Type 1 (bare-metal) — runs directly on hardware with minimal overhead and strong isolation
Type 2 (hosted) — runs on top of a desktop OS
No hypervisor — containers replace everything
Type 2 for production performance
scenarios.why: Type 1 hypervisors (ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM) sit directly on hardware: lower overhead, better isolation, built for data centers. Type 2 (VirtualBox, Workstation) rides on a host OS — fine for labs, wrong for production clusters.
scenarios.hint: What sits directly on the hardware?

scenarios.title: The VM graveyard
scenarios.situation: The cluster has 300 VMs. Nobody can say who owns forty of them, and half have not been powered on in a year.
scenarios.prompt: What is the systematic fix?
choices: Tagging with ownership, lifecycle policies, and chargeback/showback so orphans get reclaimed
Delete VMs at random
Buy more hosts
Ignore the orphans
scenarios.why: VM sprawl wastes licenses, backup windows, and attack surface. Mandatory tags (owner, purpose, expiry) plus automated reclamation workflows turn sprawl into a managed lifecycle instead of a graveyard.
scenarios.hint: Who owns that VM from 2019?

scenarios.title: VM Sluggish Despite Free Host CPU
scenarios.situation: A Linux VM on a lightly loaded ESXi host shows high application latency. Inside the guest, `top` shows 70% idle CPU, but `%steal` is consistently above 25%. The VM was recently migrated to this host. Other VMs on the same host are fine.
scenarios.prompt: What does high %steal with idle guest CPU indicate, and what should you check first?
choices: The guest kernel is misreporting; reinstall VMware Tools
CPU overcommit or a CPU limit/reservation on this VM: the hypervisor isn't scheduling its vCPUs; check resource limits and host ready-time
Memory ballooning is swapping guest pages; add more vRAM
Network contention on the vSwitch; check packet drops
scenarios.why: %steal measures time the guest wanted CPU but the hypervisor gave it to someone else. Idle guest + high steal means the VM is ready to run but isn't being scheduled — check CPU limits, reservations, shares, and ESXi CPU ready time for this VM (a limit set before migration is the classic cause). Tools (A) don't cause steal; ballooning (C) shows as swap/guest memory pressure, not steal; network (D) doesn't produce CPU steal.
scenarios.hint: Steal time means the guest is waiting on the hypervisor, not on work.

scenarios.title: Snapshot Chain Eating the Datastore
scenarios.situation: A VM's datastore usage has grown 300GB in a week although the guest reports only 40GB of new data. You find a chain of 11 snapshots, the oldest 8 months old. Deleting snapshots one by one is projected to take hours and the datastore is at 92%.
scenarios.prompt: What is the safest remediation order?
choices: Delete the oldest snapshots first to reclaim the most space immediately
Power off the VM, then delete all snapshots at once
Consolidate: use 'Delete All' so the hypervisor merges the chain in one pass, after verifying backups and free space headroom
Clone the VM to a new datastore and delete the original
scenarios.why: 'Delete All' collapses the entire delta chain into the base disk in a single consolidation pass, which is faster and safer than sequential deletes that each rewrite the chain (each intermediate delete risks a long, fragile merge). Verify a current backup first and confirm enough headroom, since consolidation needs working space. Deleting oldest-first (A) is the slowest path; powering off (B) adds downtime without changing the merge math; cloning (C) copies the bloat.
scenarios.hint: Each per-snapshot delete rewrites the chain — think about merging it once.

scenarios.title: Sorting the data zoo
scenarios.situation: A project involves three datasets: transaction records, server log files, and product photos.
scenarios.prompt: How do you classify them?
choices: Transactions are structured (rows/columns); logs are semi-structured; photos are unstructured
Everything is structured data
Everything is big data regardless of form
Classification does not matter
scenarios.why: Structured data fits relational tables; semi-structured (JSON logs) has tags but no fixed schema; unstructured (images, video) has no predefined model. The classification drives storage, tooling, and analysis choices.
scenarios.hint: Which dataset fits neatly in rows and columns?

scenarios.title: Combining the tables
scenarios.situation: You need each customer's name alongside their order totals. Customers live in one table, orders in another.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct approach?
choices: JOIN the tables on the shared customer_id key, then aggregate with GROUP BY
Run two separate queries and merge them by hand in a spreadsheet
Export both tables to CSV and eyeball it
Use SELECT * with no join condition
scenarios.why: A JOIN combines related rows via the key they share; GROUP BY with SUM then rolls orders up per customer. A join without a condition creates a Cartesian product — every customer times every order — which is never what you want.
scenarios.hint: What relates the two tables to each other?
evidence:
customers(customer_id, name)
orders(order_id, customer_id, total)
-- need: name + SUM(total) per customer

scenarios.title: Garbage in
scenarios.situation: Source systems feed your warehouse dirty data: duplicate rows, wrong date formats, nulls in required fields.
scenarios.prompt: Where do you fix it?
choices: In the ETL pipeline: validate, cleanse, and transform before loading into the warehouse
Load it raw and let analysts fix it in every report
Skip validation to load faster
Fix it by hand each morning
scenarios.why: The transform stage exists to enforce quality once, upstream: standardize formats, dedupe, reject or quarantine bad rows. Cleaning downstream means every report reinvents (and disagrees on) the fixes.
scenarios.hint: When is bad data cheapest to catch?

scenarios.title: The duplicated customer
scenarios.situation: Customer addresses are stored in every order row. A customer moves, one row gets updated, and now reports show two addresses.
scenarios.prompt: What database design principle prevents this?
choices: Normalization: store the customer once in a customer table and reference it by ID
Store even more copies for safety
Buy a bigger database
Delete the old rows by hand
scenarios.why: Update anomalies come from duplicated facts: normalization keeps each fact in one place, referenced by key, so a change happens once. Denormalization has performance uses, but it trades away this integrity.
scenarios.hint: What happens when the address changes in only one copy?

scenarios.title: Analytics on customer data
scenarios.situation: Analysts want to study purchasing patterns in production customer data that includes names, emails, and card numbers.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct handling?
choices: Mask or anonymize PII, work on the minimum necessary fields, and enforce retention limits
Give analysts raw production data — they are employees
Email CSV extracts around for convenience
No controls needed for internal use
scenarios.why: Analytics rarely needs real identities: masking/anonymization plus least-privilege access preserves utility while limiting breach impact and meeting privacy obligations. Raw PII in spreadsheets is how breaches happen.
scenarios.hint: Does the analyst need real names and card numbers?

scenarios.title: Showing the trend
scenarios.situation: Leadership wants to see monthly revenue over the past two years to judge growth.
scenarios.prompt: Which visualization is appropriate?
choices: A line chart — it shows change over continuous time
A pie chart of all 24 months
A 3D exploding pie chart
A raw data table with no chart
scenarios.why: Line charts encode time on an axis so trends, seasonality, and inflection points are visible at a glance. Pie charts compare parts of a whole at one moment — 24 slices communicate nothing about growth.
scenarios.hint: What shows change across months best?

scenarios.title: Backup That Can't Restore in Time
scenarios.situation: A file server holds 8TB. Full backups run weekly to tape, differentials nightly. The business RTO is 4 hours and RPO is 24 hours. During a drill, restoring the latest full plus six differentials took 11 hours. The backup admin proposes switching to incrementals to 'make backups faster'.
scenarios.prompt: What backup change actually meets the 4-hour RTO?
choices: Switch nightly differentials to incrementals to reduce backup windows
Move to synthetic fulls or frequent fulls on disk-based storage so restore is a single image copy, and verify with timed restore drills
Keep the current scheme but buy a faster tape drive
Replicate the file server to a warm standby instead of backups
scenarios.why: The RTO problem is restore time, not backup time: incrementals (A) make restores SLOWER (full + every incremental). A disk-based synthetic or frequent full turns restore into one sequential copy that can hit 4 hours, and only timed drills prove it. A faster tape drive (C) helps marginally but tape seek times still dominate; replication (D) is great for DR but isn't a backup — it replicates corruption and gives no point-in-time recovery.
scenarios.hint: Optimize the restore path, not the backup path — and notice what incrementals do to restores.

scenarios.title: Tiering Cold Data Without Breaking Access
scenarios.situation: A 60TB NAS is 85% full. Analysis shows 70% of files haven't been touched in 18 months, but legal requires 7-year retention and users occasionally request old project files with a 24-hour SLA. The CFO won't approve buying another shelf of fast disk.
scenarios.prompt: What storage strategy satisfies retention, access SLA, and budget?
choices: Compress everything in place and hope for 3:1 savings
Policy-based tiering: auto-move files untouched for 12+ months to cheaper object/archive storage, with transparent recall meeting the 24-hour SLA
Delete the oldest 30% and rely on legal to object if needed
Migrate the whole NAS to archive storage and accept slower access for everything
scenarios.why: Automated tiering keeps hot data on fast disk (preserving performance) while cold data lands on cheap capacity with recall inside the 24-hour SLA — exactly matching the access pattern and the retention mandate. Compression (A) is unpredictable and doesn't fix growth; deleting (C) violates legal retention; moving everything to archive (D) punishes daily users for cold data's sake.
scenarios.hint: Match storage cost to access temperature, not to the whole dataset.

scenarios.title: The database backup
scenarios.situation: A critical database is backed up nightly to disk on the same server. Restores have never been tested.
scenarios.prompt: What must change to meet a 4-hour RPO?
choices: Follow 3-2-1 with offsite copies, back up at least every 4 hours, and test restores regularly
Keep the single nightly copy — RAID protects it
Back up weekly to save space
Trust that backups work without testing
scenarios.why: RPO is the maximum tolerable data loss: a 4-hour RPO needs backups at least every 4 hours. Same-server copies die with the server (RAID is not backup), and untested restores are unproven — test on a schedule.
scenarios.hint: What does a 4-hour RPO demand of your backup frequency?

scenarios.title: Patch Tuesday for production
scenarios.situation: Security patches are released for your production hypervisors and guest servers.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct patching workflow?
choices: Test in staging first, then deploy in a maintenance window with a rollback plan
Patch production directly — speed matters most
Never patch production
Enable auto-patching on everything with no oversight
scenarios.why: Patches fix vulnerabilities but can break workloads: staging catches regressions, windows bound the blast radius, and rollback plans bound the outage. Untested production patching trades one risk for another.
scenarios.hint: Where do bad patches go first?

scenarios.title: Drowning in alerts
scenarios.situation: The monitoring system sends 500 emails a day. Engineers now ignore all of them — including real outages.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Tune thresholds, aggregate related alerts, and tier severities so critical pages are rare and real
Add more checks for coverage
Ignore everything until something breaks
Disable monitoring to stop the noise
scenarios.why: Alert fatigue is a tuning failure: when everything is critical, nothing is. Baselines drive thresholds, aggregation kills storms, and severity tiers protect the paging channel for genuine emergencies.
scenarios.hint: What happens when everything is critical?

scenarios.title: The firewall rule request
scenarios.situation: A developer needs a new firewall rule opened for a production deployment tonight.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct process?
choices: Submit a change request: business justification, risk review, approval, implementation, and verification
Add the rule now, document later
Email the firewall admin after adding it
Freeze all firewall changes forever
scenarios.why: Firewall changes alter the security boundary: they need the same change control as any production change — justification, approval, testing, and a backout plan. 'Temporary' undocumented rules become permanent holes.
scenarios.hint: What stops a temporary rule from becoming permanent?

scenarios.title: Auditing the ruleset
scenarios.situation: You inherit a firewall with 400 rules, many years old, in random order with no comments.
scenarios.prompt: What principles guide the cleanup?
choices: Default-deny, least privilege, remove unused rules, and order specific rules before general ones
Allow all traffic both directions for simplicity
Rule order does not matter
Stop logging to improve performance
scenarios.why: Firewalls evaluate top-down: specific allows/denies must precede general ones, and an explicit deny-all closes the bottom. Stale rules accumulate risk — each unused allow is an unreviewed hole. Document every rule's owner and purpose.
scenarios.hint: What should the last rule in the list be?

scenarios.title: The compromised web server
scenarios.situation: You confirm a public web server is compromised and beaconing out. It also hosts the company's main site.
scenarios.prompt: What are the correct FIRST actions?
choices: Isolate the host from the network, preserve logs and memory for forensics, and invoke the incident response plan
Keep it running to watch the attacker
Wipe and rebuild it immediately
Hide the incident to avoid embarrassment
scenarios.why: Isolation stops spread and exfiltration; preserving volatile evidence (memory, logs) enables forensics and legal action; the IR plan coordinates the rest. Wiping first destroys evidence, and watching an active compromise risks the whole network.
scenarios.hint: What does wiping destroy besides the malware?

scenarios.title: SSH Keys Everywhere
scenarios.situation: An audit finds 40 engineers with permanent SSH access to production, keys never rotated in 3 years, several ex-employees' keys still authorized, and shared 'deploy' keys in a wiki. The team deploys 20 times a day and fears any change will break the pipeline.
scenarios.prompt: What is the highest-leverage first step that doesn't halt deployments?
choices: Immediately revoke all keys and reissue per-engineer keys
Remove ex-employee keys, put the shared deploy key behind the CI system with a short-lived credential, and start key rotation with expiry
Move all SSH behind a VPN and call it done
Require hardware tokens for every SSH login starting tomorrow
scenarios.why: Kill the known-compromised credentials (ex-employees) and the highest-risk shared secret (the wiki key) first, scoping the deploy key to the CI system that actually uses it with short-lived credentials — this removes the worst exposure without touching the deploy flow. Mass revocation (A) halts deploys; a VPN (C) adds a perimeter but leaves the stolen keys valid inside; hardware tokens (D) are the end state but need a rollout plan, not a flag day.
scenarios.hint: Sequence by risk: what's already compromised, and what secret is one wiki read away from abuse?

scenarios.title: Patch Window vs. Uptime SLA
scenarios.situation: A critical kernel CVE drops on Tuesday with public exploit code. Your fleet of 200 web servers carries a 99.95% uptime SLA (about 22 minutes of monthly downtime budget). The app can't drain connections gracefully — any reboot drops in-flight requests. Security demands patching within 48 hours.
scenarios.prompt: How do you patch within 48 hours while honoring the SLA?
choices: Patch and reboot all 200 servers in one maintenance window at 2 AM
Rolling reboot in small batches behind the load balancer, draining each batch first, accepting the dropped in-flight requests on drained nodes as the cost of the window
Apply a live-patching service (e.g., kernel live patch) for the CVE now, then schedule the full reboot into the next normal window
Wait for the vendor's next scheduled patch bundle to avoid emergency churn
scenarios.why: Live patching closes the CVE exposure immediately with zero reboots, and deferring the real reboot to a planned window keeps the SLA intact. A flag-day reboot (A) blows the downtime budget and drops traffic; rolling reboots (B) still drop the in-flight requests the app can't drain; waiting (D) misses the 48-hour mandate with exploit code public.
scenarios.hint: Separate 'stop the bleeding' from 'finish the surgery' — the CVE needs closing, not necessarily a reboot.

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Comptia Infra as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The Cloud Architecture Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Cloud Architecture is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Cloud Architecture?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Cloud Architecture issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Cloud Architecture is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Cloud Architecture supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Cloud Architecture failure in Comptia Infra.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Cloud Architecture
evidence: All Cloud Architecture components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.title: The Linux Administration Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Linux Administration is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Linux Administration?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Linux Administration issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Linux Administration is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Linux Administration supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Linux Administration failure in Comptia Infra.

objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Linux Administration

Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.title: Boot Process Anatomy: Where Did It Hang?
scenarios.situation: A Linux server powers on, shows the vendor logo, then sits at a black screen with a blinking cursor — no GRUB menu, no kernel messages. The admin has already reseated the RAM. The disk activity LED never blinks.
scenarios.prompt: Using the boot sequence (firmware -> bootloader -> kernel -> init), where is the failure and what do you check?
choices: Kernel stage: boot a rescue image and rebuild the initramfs
Bootloader stage: firmware finished (logo shown) but GRUB never loaded — check boot device order, EFI boot entries, and whether the bootloader files exist
Init stage: systemd is hanging on a service; boot with systemd.unit=emergency.target
Hardware: the CPU is dead since nothing printed
scenarios.why: The vendor logo means firmware/POST completed; the disk LED staying dark and no GRUB menu means control never reached the bootloader — the failure is between firmware and bootloader. Check that the firmware is actually pointing at a bootable device (boot order, EFI NVRAM entries, GRUB files on the EFI partition). Kernel (A) and init (C) stages come later and would print messages; a dead CPU (D) wouldn't show the logo.
scenarios.hint: Map each visible symptom to exactly one handoff in the boot chain.

scenarios.title: Linux I/O Stack: Slow Disk, Fast Disk
scenarios.situation: An app reads 1GB files. `hdparm`-style raw device reads hit 500 MB/s, but the app sees 80 MB/s. `iostat` shows high await and low %util on the device. The filesystem is ext4 with default mount options, and the app does small 4KB random reads.
scenarios.prompt: Which layer of the I/O stack (app -> VFS -> page cache -> filesystem -> block layer -> driver -> device) best explains the gap?
choices: The device layer: the SSD is worn out and slow
The app/VFS layer: 4KB random reads defeat readahead and the page cache can't help first-touch data; the app should use larger sequential reads or mmap
The block layer: the I/O scheduler is misconfigured for SSDs
The filesystem: ext4 journaling is throttling reads
scenarios.why: Raw sequential device speed (500 MB/s) proves the hardware is fine — the app's 4KB random access pattern means every read is a seek-like operation with syscall overhead, and readahead/page cache can't prefetch randomly. The fix is at the app layer: bigger reads, sequential access, or mmap. The block scheduler (C) matters far less on SSDs; ext4 journaling (D) affects writes, not reads.
scenarios.hint: The device proved itself fast — so which layer transforms the app's requests into something slow?
objectives: Diagnose I/O pattern vs device capability
evidence: Attributes gap to access pattern at app layer

scenarios.title: Hypervisor Flow: The Noisy Neighbor
scenarios.situation: Two VMs share a host. VM-A runs a latency-sensitive trading app; VM-B runs nightly batch compression. When VM-B's batch starts, VM-A's p99 latency triples, though VM-A's vCPU usage stays under 40% and memory is plentiful. CPU pinning is not in use.
scenarios.prompt: Following the hypervisor scheduling flow, what is the most likely interference mechanism?
choices: VM-B is ballooning memory away from VM-A
Last-level cache and memory-bandwidth contention: VM-B's streaming workload evicts VM-A's cache lines, so VM-A stalls on memory despite idle vCPUs
VM-B's virtual disk I/O is saturating the shared datastore
The virtual switch is dropping VM-A's packets under load
scenarios.why: Idle vCPUs plus spiking latency with a streaming neighbor is the classic shared-cache/memory-bandwidth contention signature — the hypervisor schedules both fine, but VM-B's sequential streaming evicts VM-A's working set from the LLC, turning cache hits into DRAM stalls. Ballooning (A) would show guest memory pressure; datastore saturation (C) shows as disk await; vSwitch drops (D) show as packet loss, not CPU-idle latency.
scenarios.hint: The vCPUs are idle — so what shared resource below the scheduler is exhausted?

scenarios.title: Cloud Request Path: Where Did 300ms Go?
scenarios.situation: A user request to your cloud-hosted API takes 450ms; the app server logs show 120ms of processing. The path is: client -> CDN -> WAF -> load balancer -> app -> database. Each hop was 'fast when we built it' but nobody has measured per-hop since.
scenarios.prompt: What is the disciplined way to attribute the missing ~330ms across the request path?
choices: Add more app servers; the app is probably queuing
Enable distributed tracing with per-hop spans (or at minimum synchronized access logs with request IDs) and read the waterfall before changing anything
Move the database to a bigger instance since DB is usually the bottleneck
Enable CDN caching for the API responses
scenarios.why: You cannot optimize what you haven't measured per hop — distributed tracing (or correlated request-ID logs) produces a waterfall showing exactly which of CDN/WAF/LB/app/DB owns the 330ms. Guessing app (A) or DB (C) scaling wastes money if the time is in TLS handshakes at the WAF; caching (D) changes semantics and may be wrong for the endpoint. Measure the path, then fix the slowest hop.
scenarios.hint: The app already accounted for its 120ms — where's the receipt for the rest?

scenarios.title: Storage I/O Journey: Write Latency Spike
scenarios.situation: A database on a SAN sees write latency jump from 2ms to 40ms every day at 14:00 for 30 minutes. Host CPU, memory, and network are flat. The SAN admin says array cache hit rate drops during the window. Nothing in the database changes at 14:00.
scenarios.prompt: Tracing the write path (app -> filesystem -> HBA -> fabric -> array cache -> disks), where should you investigate?
choices: The app: add write-back caching in the database
Off-host: something else shares the SAN — a 14:00 backup or replication job is flooding array cache and forcing write-through to disk
The HBA: replace the fiber-channel card in the DB host
The filesystem: the journal is checkpointing at 14:00
scenarios.why: Host-side metrics are flat and the symptom is array cache hit rate collapsing on a fixed schedule — the write path is fine until the array, where a competing workload (backup snapshot, replication, another host's batch) evicts cache and forces destaging to spinning disk. Check SAN performance graphs for other initiators at 14:00. HBA (C) or journal (D) faults wouldn't follow a clock; app caching (A) papers over a shared-infrastructure problem.
scenarios.hint: The host is innocent and the clock is suspicious — who else uses the array?
evidence: Correlates schedule with array cache eviction

scenarios.title: Packet Through a Virtual Switch
scenarios.situation: VM-A can't reach VM-B on the same host and VLAN, but both reach the physical network fine. The vSwitch port groups look correct. VM-A's ARP table has no entry for VM-B, and a packet capture on VM-B's vNIC shows zero incoming packets from VM-A.
scenarios.prompt: Where in the virtual-switch path (source vNIC -> port -> vSwitch forwarding -> destination vNIC) is the packet being dropped?
choices: At the physical uplink: the upstream switch is blocking inter-VM traffic
Between source vNIC and the vSwitch, or in vSwitch policy: check promiscuous mode, MAC learning/security policy, and whether VM-A's vNIC is actually connected
At VM-B's guest firewall: it's dropping the packets silently
In the VLAN trunk: the VLAN tag is being stripped
scenarios.why: Both VMs reach the physical network, so uplinks and VLAN tagging work — and VM-B's vNIC sees nothing, ruling out its guest firewall (which would show arrivals in the capture). The drop is at the source side: a disconnected vNIC, a vSwitch security policy rejecting the MAC, or forged-transmit/MAC-change settings. ARP failing with no traffic arriving downstream localizes it before the vSwitch fabric.
scenarios.hint: VM-B's capture is the witness — nothing arrives, so eliminate everything at or after arrival.
evidence: Localizes drop to source-side vSwitch policy
