scenarios.title: PBQ: Rebuild the Broken Service
scenarios.situation: The exam presents a performance-based question: a terminal with a Linux VM where the web stack is down. You have `systemctl`, `journalctl`, `ss`, and config files. The clock shows 38 minutes left and 40 questions remaining, and this PBQ is marked as high-value.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best exam-room strategy for this PBQ?
choices: Skip it entirely — PBQs take too long and the multiple-choice questions are safer points
Spend up to 10 focused minutes: check service status, read the journal error, verify ports with ss, fix the config, then move on regardless
Solve it completely no matter how long it takes, since it's high-value
Answer the remaining multiple-choice questions first, then return with whatever time is left
scenarios.why: PBQs carry heavy weight but have diminishing returns: a disciplined 10-minute triage (status -> logs -> ports -> config) captures most partial-credit checkpoints without cannibalizing 40 other questions. Skipping (A) forfeits high-value points; unlimited time (C) starves the rest of the exam; doing all MCQs first (D) risks leaving zero time for the PBQ's easy early checkpoints.
scenarios.hint: Think in checkpoints and opportunity cost, not perfection.

scenarios.title: The 90-Second Multiple Choice
scenarios.situation: You're 25 questions into a Cloud+ exam with 75 minutes left. A long scenario stem describes a company's storage growth, compliance needs, and budget, followed by four dense answer choices. You've already re-read the stem twice and two choices both look plausible.
scenarios.prompt: What should you do right now?
choices: Keep re-reading until you're certain — accuracy beats speed
Flag it, pick your best instinct, and move on; return only if time remains after the first pass
Eliminate the two implausible choices and guess randomly between the remaining two
Skip it with no answer to avoid a wrong-answer penalty
scenarios.why: Banked time is the scarcest exam resource: flag-and-move preserves momentum and your subconscious keeps working on it, while a second pass with fresh eyes often resolves the ambiguity. Re-reading (A) burns minutes for marginal gain; there's no wrong-answer penalty on CompTIA exams so (D) is pure loss; and (C) is fine as the instinct pick inside the flag-and-move, not as the whole strategy.
scenarios.hint: The exam rewards completed passes over perfect single questions.

scenarios.title: Troubleshooting Methodology Under Pressure
scenarios.situation: A PBQ drops you into a broken three-tier app: users can't log in. You have 8 minutes budgeted. Logs show the web tier returning 500s, the app tier logging 'connection refused' to the database, and the database host responding to ping.
scenarios.prompt: Following a top-down vs bottom-up methodology, what is the correct next step?
choices: Restart the database — connection refused means it's down
Bottom-up: verify the DB service is listening (ss/netstat on the DB host), then check firewall rules and credentials layer by layer
Top-down: rewrite the web tier's connection string first since 500s start there
Check DNS resolution between tiers
scenarios.why: The evidence localizes the break between app and DB ('connection refused' = reached host, nothing listening or blocked). Bottom-up verification — is the DB process listening on the expected port, then is the path clear (firewall), then are credentials valid — tests each layer exactly once. Restarting (A) is a guess that destroys evidence; starting at the web tier (C) works the wrong end; DNS (D) would give resolution errors, not connection refused.
scenarios.hint: 'Connection refused' already tells you the network path works — what's the next layer?

scenarios.title: Reading Logs Against the Clock
scenarios.situation: A PBQ gives you a 400-line log file and asks which service caused an outage. Timestamps show errors cascading across web, cache, and database services within 90 seconds. You have 6 minutes left on your PBQ budget.
scenarios.prompt: How do you find the root cause fast?
choices: Read the log top to bottom carefully
Jump to the FIRST error in chronological order — cascades propagate forward, so the earliest failure is the likely root cause
Search for the most frequent error — volume indicates the culprit
Check the last lines — the final error is what killed the system
scenarios.why: Cascading failures propagate forward in time: the web tier's errors at 10:02 are effects of the database's first failure at 10:00. The earliest anomaly is the root-cause candidate; everything after is fallout. Reading linearly (A) wastes the budget; frequency (C) just measures which service complains loudest; the last line (D) is the final victim, not the cause.
scenarios.hint: Causes precede effects — sort by time, not by volume.
evidence: Finds earliest error as root cause

scenarios.title: Parsing the Scenario Stem
scenarios.situation: A question stem is a full paragraph: a hospital needs a new backup system; HIPAA compliance is mentioned; RTO 2 hours; the WAN link is 100 Mbps; the answer choices are four backup architectures. You've seen similar questions where one detail is a distractor.
scenarios.prompt: What is the reliable way to extract what the question actually tests?
choices: Read the last sentence first to find the actual question, then scan the stem only for constraints that discriminate between choices
Memorize every detail — the exam punishes missed facts
Pick the choice mentioning HIPAA since compliance was emphasized
Choose the most technically advanced architecture
scenarios.why: The final sentence defines the decision being asked; the stem's job is to supply discriminating constraints (RTO 2h over a 100 Mbps WAN rules out off-site full restores). Reading question-first prevents distractor details (HIPAA matters for encryption, not for the architecture choice here) from anchoring you. Memorizing everything (B) wastes time; keyword-matching (C) and tech-shine (D) are classic wrong-answer traps.
scenarios.hint: The question is at the end; the constraints are the filter.

scenarios.title: Command-Line PBQ: Fix the Network
scenarios.situation: PBQ: a Linux VM has no network. `ip addr` shows the interface UP with no IP address. `ip route` is empty. There's a DHCP server on the network and the exam gives you root. You've budgeted 7 minutes.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fastest correct fix sequence?
choices: Assign a static IP with ip addr add, add a default route, and write resolv.conf
Restart the whole VM and hope DHCP works on boot
Run dhclient (or systemctl restart the DHCP client / NetworkManager) to request a lease, then verify with ip addr
Edit /etc/network/interfaces and reboot the networking service twice
scenarios.why: Interface UP with no address and an empty route table on a DHCP network means the DHCP client never completed — re-running dhclient (or restarting NetworkManager/systemd-networkd) requests a fresh lease in seconds, which is the minimal fix matching the environment. Static config (A) works but fights the stated DHCP design and takes longer; rebooting (B/D) wastes minutes on an 7-minute budget.
scenarios.hint: Match the fix to the environment's design: DHCP network, DHCP-shaped symptom.

scenarios.title: When Two Answers Both Work
scenarios.situation: A scenario asks for the BEST way to secure management access to 50 switches. Choice B (SSH with key auth) and choice D (a jump host with MFA) are both genuinely good practices. You've narrowed it to these two with 60 seconds spent.
scenarios.prompt: How do you break the tie?
choices: Pick the longer, more detailed answer — exams reward completeness
Re-read the stem for scale/scope words (50 switches, management access): the BEST answer is the one that scales and centralizes — the jump host with MFA
Pick B because SSH keys are the more fundamental skill
Always pick the answer mentioning MFA — security questions want MFA
scenarios.why: CompTIA 'BEST/MOST' questions are decided by the stem's scope constraints: at 50 switches, per-device SSH keys become a management nightmare while a jump host centralizes access control, auditing, and MFA in one place. Length (A) and keyword superstitions (C, D) are traps; the tiebreaker is always which choice the stem's scale and constraints uniquely favor.
scenarios.hint: BEST means 'best given the stem's scale' — whose advantage grows with 50 devices?

scenarios.title: The Final 15 Minutes
scenarios.situation: Fifteen minutes remain. You have 6 flagged questions, one half-finished PBQ (you fixed the service but didn't verify), and 3 unanswered questions at the end you never reached. Your first-pass instinct answers are marked on the flagged ones.
scenarios.prompt: What is the optimal order of operations?
choices: Finish the PBQ verification first, then flagged questions, then the unanswered
Answer the 3 unanswered questions first (a blank is a guaranteed zero), then the PBQ verification, then flagged review with remaining time
Review all flagged questions carefully — they're the ones you were unsure about
Redo the PBQ from scratch to make sure the fix was right
scenarios.why: Expected-value ordering: unanswered questions are guaranteed zeros — even 30-second instinct answers have positive expected value. The PBQ verification is a cheap checkpoint for partial credit. Flagged review comes last because first instincts are statistically strong and re-litigating risks changing right answers to wrong ones under time pressure. Redoing the PBQ (D) is the worst time investment.
scenarios.hint: Rank by expected points per minute: zeros first, cheap verifications second.

domains.name: Capacity Planning & Sizing
domains.description: Right-size compute, memory, storage, and network before you buy — the skill that saves budgets and outages.

scenarios.title: The VM That Crawls at 9 AM
scenarios.situation: Every morning at 9 AM, the terminal server VM becomes unusable for 30 minutes. CPU shows 95%, memory is fine, disk latency is normal. The host has 8 other VMs.
scenarios.prompt: Diagnose using the resource-output discipline. What is the most likely cause and the correct fix?
choices: Memory exhaustion — add RAM to the VM immediately

CPU contention from noisy neighbors or overcommitment: check host-level ready-time/CPU wait; the 9 AM pattern suggests scheduled tasks or logon storms colliding — stagger schedules or add host capacity / reduce vCPUs
Disk bottleneck — move the VM to faster storage
Network saturation — the morning logon storm floods the vSwitch
scenarios.why: CPU at 95% with memory and disk healthy isolates the bottleneck to compute — but is it the VM's workload or host contention? The 9 AM pattern plus 8 co-tenants points at contention: check host CPU ready-time. If ready-time is high, the host is overcommitted — the fix is host capacity or vCPU right-sizing, not feeding the VM more of a contested resource. Disk latency normal rules out storage; memory fine rules out swap.
scenarios.hint: CPU is high — but whose CPU? The VM's, or the host's shared pool? What metric distinguishes them?

scenarios.title: The Database Storage Decision
scenarios.situation: A new SQL Server needs 6TB usable, high write throughput, and must survive one disk failure. Budget allows 12TB raw on SSD. The vendor suggests RAID 5 'for capacity efficiency'.
scenarios.prompt: Evaluate the recommendation. What should you choose?
choices: Accept RAID 5 — the vendor knows their arrays, and capacity efficiency matters

RAID 10: 12TB raw → 6TB usable, survives 1+ disk failures (per mirror), best write performance for database workloads. RAID 5's write penalty (4 I/Os per write) compounds under DB load — reject the vendor's suggestion with the math
RAID 0 — fastest option, and backups cover the risk
RAID 6 — maximum fault tolerance is always the right answer
scenarios.why: Databases are write-heavy; RAID 5's write penalty (read-modify-write = 4 backend I/Os per host write) strangles DB throughput under load. RAID 10 gives exactly 6TB usable from 12TB raw, survives disk failures per mirror pair, and delivers the best write IOPS. RAID 6 wastes capacity here and adds latency. The vendor optimized for their margin (fewer disks), not your workload — the trade-off table is your defense.
scenarios.hint: What does a database do most — reads or writes? What does RAID 5 do to writes?
evidence: 6TB usable, high write IOPS, 1-disk fault tolerance, 12TB raw SSD budget
RAID 5 across 6x 2TB: ~10TB usable 'with room to grow'

scenarios.title: Right-Sizing an Over-Provisioned Fleet
scenarios.situation: Your 120-VM fleet averages 18% CPU and 35% memory utilization. Finance flags the cloud bill; engineering fears performance regressions if you downsize. The workloads are a mix of steady web servers and spiky batch jobs, and you have 90 days of per-VM metrics.
scenarios.prompt: What is the defensible right-sizing approach?
choices: Downsize every VM one size and watch for complaints
Downsize based on p95 (not average) utilization per VM, keep batch jobs on burstable classes, and stage the change with rollback per workload group
Do nothing — headroom is the point of the cloud
Move everything to the smallest instance size to maximize savings
scenarios.why: Averages hide peaks: p95 sizing preserves headroom for real spikes while still capturing most of the waste, burstable classes match spiky batch economics, and staged rollout with rollback answers engineering's regression fear with evidence. Blanket downsizing (A/D) risks peak-hour outages; doing nothing (C) ignores the data you already paid to collect.
scenarios.hint: Averages lie about peaks — which percentile tells the truth about needed headroom?

scenarios.title: Forecasting Holiday Traffic
scenarios.situation: Last Black Friday, traffic was 6x normal and the site degraded at 4x. This year marketing expects 8x with a new product launch. You have three years of hourly traffic data showing 40% year-over-year peak growth. Infrastructure lead time for new capacity is 3 weeks.
scenarios.prompt: How much capacity do you provision, and when?
choices: Provision for 8x now — marketing's number is the requirement
Provision for 10-12x (8x forecast plus headroom), completed 4+ weeks before the event, validated with a load test at the target
Provision for 6x like last year and auto-scale the rest
Wait until the week before, then provision based on pre-sale numbers
scenarios.why: Forecast (8x, consistent with 40% YoY growth on 6x) plus explicit headroom (failures happen at peak) gives 10-12x; finishing 4+ weeks early beats the 3-week lead time and leaves room for the load test that actually proves the number. Marketing's number (A) has no safety margin; 6x (C) repeats last year's degradation; waiting (D) collides with lead time.
scenarios.hint: Forecast plus headroom, minus lead time — what date does that math give you?

scenarios.title: Finding the Real Bottleneck
scenarios.situation: Checkout latency doubled after a traffic increase. CPU is at 45%, memory at 60%, disk await is normal, but the app server's connection pool to the database is saturated and DB CPU is at 95% with lock waits climbing.
scenarios.prompt: Where is the bottleneck, and what proves it?
choices: The app servers — add more to spread the load
The database: saturated connection pool plus 95% DB CPU with lock waits shows the DB can't serve the offered load; app CPU is idle because threads wait on the DB
The network — latency doubled, so packets are being lost
The disk — databases are always disk-bound
scenarios.why: The saturated pool and 95% DB CPU with lock waits are direct evidence the database is the constraint; app servers at 45% CPU are starved, not overloaded — adding app servers (A) just adds more waiters to the same saturated pool. Disk await is normal (ruling out D) and there's no packet-loss evidence (C). Fix the DB: query optimization, indexing, read replicas, or connection pooling.
scenarios.hint: Which component's queue is full while the others sit idle?

scenarios.title: Scale Up or Scale Out?
scenarios.situation: A stateful legacy application is hitting CPU limits on its single large VM. The vendor supports active-passive clustering with a 30-second failover. Rewriting for horizontal scale would take 6 months. Traffic grows 10% per quarter.
scenarios.prompt: What scaling decision fits the constraints?
choices: Scale out immediately with a load balancer — horizontal is always better
Scale up (bigger VM) now for headroom, and run the vendor's active-passive cluster for availability; revisit scale-out with the rewrite
Do nothing and let the vendor handle performance
Shard the database across multiple VMs this weekend
scenarios.why: The app is stateful and the vendor only supports active-passive — scale-out (A) would break session state and void support, and sharding (D) is a rewrite in disguise. Scaling up buys quarters of headroom at 10% growth while the supported cluster covers availability; the real scale-out waits for the 6-month rewrite. Doing nothing (C) lets growth eat the remaining headroom.
scenarios.hint: What does the vendor actually support, and what does statefulness forbid?
evidence: Justifies scale-up given stateful vendor limits

scenarios.title: Cost vs Performance: The Database Tier
scenarios.situation: The analytics database runs on premium SSD storage at $4,000/month. Profiling shows 90% of queries hit the last 30 days of data; older data is queried rarely but must stay online per policy. Moving cold data to standard storage cuts the bill to $1,200/month with a 3x latency hit on cold queries.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right cost-performance trade?
choices: Keep everything on premium SSD — performance is never worth risking
Tier by age: last 90 days on premium SSD, older data on standard storage; 90% of queries keep full speed and the bill drops ~60%
Move everything to standard storage and accept the latency
Delete data older than a year to shrink the bill
scenarios.why: Access temperature maps cleanly to storage tiers: the hot 30-day working set keeps premium performance for 90% of queries while cold data's 3x latency is invisible in practice since it's rarely touched — and policy retention is preserved. All-premium (A) wastes money on cold bytes; all-standard (C) punishes the hot path; deletion (D) violates retention policy.
scenarios.hint: Which queries pay the latency price, and how often do they run?

scenarios.title: Alert Thresholds That Don't Cry Wolf
scenarios.situation: The ops team gets 200 CPU alerts a week; 95% are transient spikes that self-resolve. Real incidents have been missed because engineers mute the channel. The service can tolerate 5 minutes of high CPU, but sustained 85%+ for 15 minutes precedes outages.
scenarios.prompt: How do you set thresholds that catch real problems without the noise?
choices: Lower the threshold to 70% so nothing is ever missed
Alert on sustained 85%+ for 15 minutes (matching the known failure precursor), and convert transient spikes to a dashboard, not pages
Disable CPU alerts entirely and rely on user complaints
Page on any single 90% reading to be safe
scenarios.why: Alert on the failure precursor you actually observed (85% for 15 min), not on raw spikes — duration-based thresholds filter transients while catching the real pattern, and dashboards preserve visibility without paging. Lowering (A) or single-reading (D) thresholds multiplies the noise that caused the muting; disabling (C) blinds you. Alert fatigue is a reliability bug; fix the signal.
scenarios.hint: You know the exact precursor pattern — alert on that, not on CPU in general.
evidence: Sets duration-based threshold from observed precursor

domains.name: Hybrid Cloud Architecture
domains.description: Connect on-premises and cloud as one system: identity, networking, data flow, and the operational seams.

scenarios.title: The Backup That Wasn't
scenarios.situation: Ransomware hit the file server. The team goes to restore from last night's cloud backup — and discovers the backup job has been failing silently for 3 weeks. The local backup is encrypted too.
scenarios.prompt: What failed, and what is the immediate path forward?
choices: The backup software is broken — reinstall it and restore

Monitoring and 3-2-1 discipline failed: no alerting on job failure, no isolated/offline copy. Immediate: engage IR, assess ransom vs rebuild decision with leadership; do NOT pay without counsel. Permanent: monitored backups, tested restores, isolated offline copy
The cloud provider lost the data — open a support ticket
Restore from the local backup — ransomware rarely encrypts everything
scenarios.why: An unmonitored backup is not a backup — it is a hope. The failure is operational: no alerting on job status, no restore testing, no isolated copy per 3-2-1. Immediate path is incident response (scope, counsel, business decision on recovery options — never pay without legal/executive decision). The permanent fix is boring and non-negotiable: alert on every failed job, test-restores monthly, one offline/immutable copy.
scenarios.hint: What is the difference between a backup job existing and a backup existing? Which one did they have?
evidence: Last successful cloud backup: 21 days ago. 20 consecutive failures, no alerts configured.

scenarios.title: Hybrid DNS: The Quiet Breakage
scenarios.situation: After connecting the new branch via site-to-site VPN to Azure, on-prem users cannot reach cloud VMs by name, but IP connectivity works. Cloud VMs resolve on-prem names fine.
scenarios.prompt: Where is the seam broken, and what is the fix?
choices: The VPN tunnel is misconfigured — rebuild it

One-way DNS: conditional forwarders exist cloud→on-prem but not on-prem→cloud (or the on-prem DNS cannot reach the Azure DNS forwarder through the tunnel). Fix: configure on-prem conditional forwarder for the Azure zone pointing at the Azure DNS IP, verify UDP/TCP 53 through the tunnel
Azure VMs need public IPs for name resolution
The on-prem DNS server is down
scenarios.why: IP works + one direction resolves = the network seam is fine; the DNS seam is half-built. Name resolution across a hybrid boundary needs forwarders in BOTH directions (or a unified design). The asymmetric symptom (cloud→on-prem works, reverse fails) points exactly at the missing on-prem→cloud conditional forwarder — or a firewall rule blocking DNS through the tunnel in that direction. Always verify port 53 both ways through the tunnel.
scenarios.hint: Traffic flows one way for IPs but names fail asymmetrically. Which seam carries names?
evidence: On-prem client → cloudvm.corp.local: NXDOMAIN. Ping 10.2.0.4: replies.
On-prem DNS: forwarder for azure.corp.local — missing. Cloud DNS: forwarder for corp.local — present.

scenarios.title: Where Does This Workload Live?
scenarios.situation: A hospital runs a patient-scheduling app (steady load, PHI data, strict audit rules) and a research analytics pipeline (spiky, de-identified data, needs 200 GPUs for 6 hours weekly). The CIO wants a hybrid strategy but the team is split: 'everything on-prem for compliance' vs 'everything in cloud for agility'.
scenarios.prompt: What workload placement best serves both requirements?
choices: Everything on-prem: compliance demands it
Everything in cloud: agility demands it
Scheduling stays on-prem (steady, PHI, audit-friendly); analytics bursts to cloud GPUs (spiky, de-identified, pay-per-use)
Split both workloads 50/50 across on-prem and cloud for redundancy
scenarios.why: Placement follows workload shape: the steady PHI system gains nothing from cloud elasticity and stays where audit controls exist; the spiky GPU pipeline would force buying 200 idle GPUs on-prem, while cloud pay-per-use matches its 6-hour weekly shape and the data is de-identified. Absolutist options (A/B) optimize one workload at the other's expense; 50/50 (D) doubles operational burden with no rationale.
scenarios.hint: Match each workload's shape (steady vs spiky, PHI vs de-identified) to the platform's economics.
objectives: Place workloads by shape and sensitivity

scenarios.title: Migration Wave Sequencing
scenarios.situation: You're migrating 80 applications to cloud over a year. The inventory: 10 stateless web apps, 30 internal tools with local file dependencies, 25 tightly-coupled legacy client-server apps, and 15 regulated apps requiring re-certification after any move. Leadership wants 'quick wins' in Q1.
scenarios.prompt: What wave order minimizes risk while showing early progress?
choices: Migrate the 25 legacy client-server apps first — hardest first
Wave 1: the 10 stateless web apps (easy wins, prove the pipeline); Wave 2: internal tools after remediating file dependencies; legacy and regulated last with dedicated plans
Migrate all 80 in parallel to finish in one quarter
Start with the 15 regulated apps to get compliance out of the way
scenarios.why: Stateless web apps are low-risk, high-learning migrations that prove the landing zone, networking, and runbooks — the 'quick wins' leadership wants. Internal tools need dependency remediation first; legacy coupling and re-certification are the long poles that deserve dedicated waves, not rushed starts. Hardest-first (A) risks a year-one failure; parallel (C) exceeds team capacity; regulated-first (D) burns the timeline on certification.
scenarios.hint: Which wave teaches the team the migration pattern at the lowest blast radius?
evidence: Orders waves by risk and learning

scenarios.title: Connectivity: VPN vs Direct Link
scenarios.situation: The datacenter must connect to the cloud region for a hybrid database cluster with synchronous replication. The replication needs 2 Gbps sustained and under 5ms latency variance. A site-to-site VPN over the 1 Gbps internet link is already configured and 'works fine' for admin traffic.
scenarios.prompt: What connectivity choice meets the replication requirements?
choices: Keep the VPN — it's already working and free
Provision a dedicated private interconnect (Direct Connect / ExpressRoute class) sized for 2+ Gbps with an SLA, and keep the VPN as backup
Bond two VPN tunnels for 2 Gbps
Switch replication to asynchronous so the VPN suffices
scenarios.why: Synchronous replication with tight latency variance needs deterministic private connectivity — a dedicated interconnect provides committed bandwidth and an SLA, which internet VPNs can't guarantee (jitter kills sync replication). Bonded VPNs (C) add bandwidth but not latency determinism; async replication (D) changes the RPO contract silently; the existing VPN (A) meets admin needs, not replication needs.
scenarios.hint: Synchronous replication fails on jitter, not just on average speed.
objectives: Match network SLA to replication mode
evidence: Requires dedicated link for sync replication

scenarios.title: Identity Federation Across the Divide
scenarios.situation: Engineers now manage resources both on-prem (Active Directory) and in two cloud providers. They're juggling three sets of credentials; helpdesk tickets for password resets doubled. Security found shared admin accounts in the cloud consoles. The CISO mandates MFA everywhere and no standing cloud admin credentials.
scenarios.prompt: What identity architecture fixes this?
choices: Create matching local accounts in each cloud with strong passwords
Federate: AD as the identity provider via SAML/OIDC to both clouds, enforce MFA at the IdP, and replace standing admin credentials with just-in-time elevation
Give everyone the shared admin accounts but add MFA to them
Sync passwords from AD to the clouds nightly
scenarios.why: Federation gives one identity, one MFA enforcement point, and no cloud-local passwords to phish or share — plus JIT elevation eliminates the standing admin credentials the CISO banned. Mirrored accounts (A) triple the credential sprawl; shared admins with MFA (C) still share the credential; password sync (D) propagates AD passwords into two more breach surfaces.
scenarios.hint: One identity, enforced once — where should the MFA decision live?
evidence: Designs SAML/OIDC federation with JIT admin

scenarios.title: Data Gravity Pulls Back
scenarios.situation: The team moved analytics compute to the cloud but left the 40TB data warehouse on-prem. Every nightly job pulls 3TB across the interconnect, jobs miss their SLA, and egress/transfer costs spiked. The architect suggests 'just get a bigger pipe'.
scenarios.prompt: What actually solves the data-gravity problem?
choices: Buy a bigger interconnect — bandwidth fixes everything
Move the compute to the data or the data to the compute: replicate the warehouse to cloud storage near the analytics cluster (or run analytics on-prem)
Compress the 3TB transfer to make it fit the window
Run the jobs less often
scenarios.why: Data gravity means the 40TB dataset dictates placement — compute must sit next to the data or the data must move once (replication) instead of 3TB nightly forever. A bigger pipe (A) treats the symptom at recurring cost; compression (C) is marginal against terabytes; reducing frequency (D) degrades the business SLA. Co-locate compute and data, then the transfer problem disappears.
scenarios.hint: The 3TB moves every night — what if it only had to move once?
evidence: Proposes one-time replication over nightly transfer

scenarios.title: DR Across Clouds
scenarios.situation: Primary runs in Cloud A (us-east). The board wants DR that survives a full Cloud A regional failure, with RTO 4 hours and RPO 1 hour for the order system. The team proposes warm standby in Cloud A us-west — 'different region, same cloud, half the work'.
scenarios.prompt: Does the us-west plan meet the requirement, and if not, what does?
choices: Yes — different region satisfies DR
No: same-cloud DR shares control-plane and vendor-wide failure modes; use warm standby in Cloud B with cross-cloud replication and tested failover runbooks
No — but active-active across Cloud A regions is enough
Yes, as long as backups are copied to us-west
scenarios.why: The requirement is surviving a Cloud A regional failure — but region-wide cloud incidents (control plane, IAM, DNS) routinely span regions of the same provider. True isolation needs a second provider (Cloud B) with independent control plane, plus replication that actually meets RPO 1h and runbooks tested against the 4h RTO. Same-cloud options (A/C) and backups alone (D, which can't meet a 4h RTO restore) miss the failure mode.
scenarios.hint: What failures take down two regions of one cloud at once?
evidence: Rejects same-cloud DR for shared control plane

domains.name: Automation & Infrastructure as Code
domains.description: Stop clicking consoles: templates, configuration management, and the discipline of immutable infrastructure.

scenarios.title: The Server That Drifted
scenarios.situation: The Ansible playbook says all web servers run NTP with the corporate servers. An audit finds web-07 using pool.ntp.org and a manual config edit from 6 months ago. The playbook 'runs clean' weekly.
scenarios.prompt: What happened, and how do you fix it durably?
choices: Ansible is broken — reinstall it on web-07

Configuration drift with a non-enforcing run: the playbook likely runs in check-only or the NTP task is not idempotent/enforced (e.g., notify handler never fires, or the task was removed). Fix: make the task enforcing and idempotent, run with --check first to preview, investigate why drift was not corrected — then re-run across the fleet
Someone hacked web-07 — isolate it immediately
NTP does not matter — close the audit finding
scenarios.why: A 'clean' run that permits drift is not enforcing desired state — the task is either check-only, scoped wrong, or the handler chain is broken. The durable fix has two parts: repair the playbook task (idempotent, enforcing, handler wired) and find the process gap (why did a manual edit survive 6 months of runs?). Drift is entropy; config management is the counter-force — but only when it actually enforces.
scenarios.hint: The playbook runs clean AND the server is wrong. What does that tell you about the run mode?
evidence: web-07: ntp.conf server pool.ntp.org; mtime 6 months ago; comment '# temp fix - JS'
Weekly run: OK, 0 changed on web-07 for 24 consecutive runs.

scenarios.title: Should This Be Automated?
scenarios.situation: A senior engineer wants to automate the quarterly firewall rule review: it takes 4 hours, involves judgment calls about business justification, and the rules change based on audit findings. Meanwhile, VM provisioning (30 min, 40x/month, identical steps) is still manual and error-prone.
scenarios.prompt: Where should automation effort go first?
choices: Automate the firewall review — senior work deserves automation
Automate VM provisioning first: high frequency x consistent steps x current errors = the best ROI; assist (not replace) the judgment-heavy firewall review
Automate both in parallel
Automate neither — automation always introduces risk
scenarios.why: Automation ROI = frequency x consistency x error cost. Provisioning (40x/month, identical, error-prone) is the textbook target; the firewall review is infrequent, judgment-heavy, and variable — automate the data-gathering around it but keep the human decision. Automating judgment work first (A) encodes bad decisions at speed; parallel (C) splits focus; (D) ignores the provisioning errors already costing the team.
scenarios.hint: Multiply frequency by consistency — which task scores higher?
evidence: Ranks provisioning over review by ROI

scenarios.title: The Script That Worked Twice
scenarios.situation: A deployment script creates a VM, attaches a disk, and installs the app. Run once, it works. Run twice (after a partial failure), it creates a duplicate VM and fails attaching the disk. The team now 'just knows' to clean up manually before re-running.
scenarios.prompt: What principle is violated, and what is the fix?
choices: The script needs more logging
Idempotency: the script must check current state first (VM exists? disk attached? app installed?) and converge toward desired state instead of blindly executing steps
The script needs to run faster so partial failures don't happen
Manual cleanup is fine — document it in the runbook
scenarios.why: Non-idempotent scripts turn every retry into a new mess — the fix is state checks before each action so re-runs converge instead of duplicating. Logging (A) observes the problem without fixing it; speed (C) doesn't prevent partial failures; manual cleanup (D) institutionalizes the fragility. Idempotency is what makes automation safe to retry, which is the whole point of automating recovery.
scenarios.hint: What should the second run do differently from the first?

scenarios.title: State File Showdown
scenarios.situation: Two engineers run Terraform against the same environment from their laptops. After a week, `terraform plan` shows it wants to destroy and recreate the production database — neither engineer changed the DB config. The state file lives on a shared drive with no locking.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong, and what is the correct state management?
choices: Terraform is buggy with databases; manage the DB manually instead
Concurrent runs with an unlocked, shared state file caused state drift/corruption; move to remote state backend with locking (e.g., S3 + DynamoDB / Terraform Cloud) and one pipeline
Delete the state file and re-import everything
Have the engineers coordinate over chat before running Terraform
scenarios.why: Without locking, two writers interleave state updates — each engineer's local run bases its plan on a stale/corrupted view, producing phantom destroy plans. Remote state with locking serializes access and makes the state the single source of truth; running through one CI pipeline removes the laptop variance. Manual management (A) abandons IaC; re-import (C) is painful and doesn't prevent recurrence; chat coordination (D) doesn't scale and already failed.
scenarios.hint: Two writers, no lock — what happens to the shared record of truth?
evidence: Moves to locked remote state + pipeline

scenarios.title: Secrets in the Repo
scenarios.situation: A code search finds a production database password in a Terraform variables file committed 6 months ago, plus an API key in a CI log. The repo is private 'so it's fine' according to the team. The password hasn't been rotated since.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct remediation sequence?
choices: Delete the commit from git history and move on
Rotate the exposed credentials immediately, purge them from history, move secrets to a vault with dynamic/short-lived credentials, and scan for other exposures
Make the repo more private with stricter access controls
Rotate the password next quarter during the scheduled rotation
scenarios.why: Exposed secrets are compromised secrets — rotation comes FIRST because history rewrites don't un-expose anything (clones and logs already escaped). Then purge history, move to a secrets manager with short-lived dynamic credentials so future leaks self-expire, and scan for more. History surgery alone (A) leaves the live password valid; tighter repo ACLs (C) don't revoke what's out; waiting (D) leaves a known-compromised credential active.
scenarios.hint: The secret has been readable for 6 months — what must happen before any cleanup matters?

scenarios.title: Rollback Plan for the Big Apply
scenarios.situation: Friday 4 PM: a Terraform apply will replace 30 production VMs with a new image containing an OS upgrade. The plan looks clean. The change window is 2 hours and the team has no tested rollback — 'we can just re-apply the old config if needed'.
scenarios.prompt: What should happen before anyone approves this apply?
choices: Approve it — the plan is clean and re-apply is a valid rollback
Require: a tested rollback (previous image kept bootable, data backup verified), staged rollout (canary group first), and a go/no-go checkpoint — or defer to Monday
Apply it now but have everyone on video call
Skip the OS upgrade entirely to avoid risk
scenarios.why: 'Re-apply the old config' is not a rollback plan — re-applying takes as long as the forward change, may not restore data state, and is untested under pressure. A real plan keeps the old image bootable, verifies backups, rolls in stages with a canary, and defines the abort criteria upfront. Friday 4 PM with a 2-hour window and no plan is how outages become weekend outages. More eyes (C) don't create a plan; skipping (D) avoids this risk by accepting all future CVE risk.
scenarios.hint: How long does the 'rollback' actually take, and has anyone ever run it?

scenarios.title: GitOps Gone Sideways
scenarios.situation: The team adopted GitOps: git is the source of truth, an agent syncs the cluster. But engineers keep `kubectl apply`-ing hotfixes directly 'just this once', and now git and the cluster disagree. The agent is set to auto-sync, and last night it reverted a hotfix that was keeping payments up.
scenarios.prompt: How do you restore GitOps discipline without breaking the on-call's ability to respond?
choices: Disable auto-sync so hotfixes survive
Keep auto-sync; require hotfixes to go through git (even expedited PRs), make the agent's diff visible/alerting, and give on-call a documented emergency git path
Let engineers keep using kubectl and sync git from the cluster periodically
Remove the GitOps agent and go back to manual kubectl
scenarios.why: GitOps only works if git is the single writer — every kubectl hotfix is a fork of the truth that auto-sync will eventually clobber (as payments learned). The answer isn't disabling sync (A) but making the git path fast enough for emergencies: expedited PRs, visible diffs, and a practiced emergency flow. Syncing git from the cluster (C) inverts the model; removing the agent (D) surrenders the consistency GitOps bought.
scenarios.hint: The agent did exactly what it was told — so which writer broke the contract?
evidence: Routes hotfixes through git with expedited path

scenarios.title: Testing the Untestable Infra Code
scenarios.situation: The Terraform modules manage production networking. There are no tests — 'you can't test infrastructure'. Last month a module change opened an overly broad security group in production. The team wants tests but fears slowing down delivery.
scenarios.prompt: What testing strategy fits infrastructure code without grinding delivery to a halt?
choices: No tests — manual review is enough for infra code
Layered: static analysis + policy-as-code checks (e.g., no 0.0.0.0/0 ingress) on every PR, plan-output review, and ephemeral-environment smoke tests for network modules
Full production mirror environment for every PR
Only test after deploying to production and watching metrics
scenarios.why: Policy-as-code on every PR would have caught the 0.0.0.0/0 rule in seconds at near-zero cost; plan review catches logic errors; ephemeral environments validate the risky modules without a permanent mirror. Manual review alone (A) already failed; a full mirror per PR (C) is prohibitively slow/expensive; testing in prod (D) is how the incident happened. Fast cheap gates on every change, expensive gates where risk justifies them.
scenarios.hint: Which check would have caught the open security group in under a minute?

IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS: the line moves up the stack with PaaS and SaaS, but IaaS guests are always the customer's job.
Auto-scaling matches capacity to demand automatically, and the load balancer spreads traffic across the fleet.
Storage types: object storage is built for massive numbers of flat, immutable blobs (images, backups) with HTTP access; databases need low-latency block devices that look like local disks.

lessons.title: CompTIA Infrastructure (Network+/Server+ Track) — Core concepts
concepts: IP addressing is hierarchical: the subnet mask splits every address into network and host portions. Two hosts communicate directly only when they share a network — otherwise traffic goes through the gateway.
Subnet math is powers of two: borrowing n bits creates 2^n subnets with 2^(32-n) - 2 usable hosts each. A /26 carved from a /24 yields four subnets of 62 usable hosts.

Switches versus routers: switches forward within a broadcast domain using MAC tables; routers separate broadcast domains and forward between networks using IP routing tables. VLANs need a router (or layer-3 switch) to talk to each other.
DNS and DHCP are the invisible infrastructure: DHCP automates addressing (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge); DNS translates names. When the internet is 'down' but IPs ping, suspect DNS.

Virtualization abstracts hardware: a type-1 hypervisor runs on bare metal for production servers; type-2 runs atop an OS for labs and desktops. VMs share physical NICs and storage through virtual switches and datastores.

Storage protocols fit workloads: block storage (iSCSI, Fibre Channel) for databases and VM datastores needing raw disks; file storage (SMB, NFS) for shared files; object storage for scale-out unstructured data.

example.code:
ip -brief addr show
ip route show default
example.walkthrough: The first command shows each interface's IP address and mask; the second shows the default gateway. If the address and mask are right but the gateway is missing or wrong, the LAN works and the internet does not.

pitfalls: Common trap: assigning the network or broadcast address to a host — for example .0 or .255 in a /24.
Common trap: confusing a switch with a router — adding another switch never fixes an inter-VLAN routing problem.
Common trap: overlapping subnets on VPN tunnels — identical ranges on both sides break routing.
Common trap: forgetting DNS — 'can't reach the site by name but the IP works' is a DNS problem, not a routing problem.

Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: The study order is deliberate — follow it: Start Here first, then work each domain in listed order. Domains unlock as you demonstrate mastery, because Cloud+ / Server+ topics build on each other.
What 'terminal' means: the Terminal tab is a real shell where labs run. Every lab command executes there — you learn by doing, not by reading about doing.
Lessons teach concepts with a worked example, pitfalls, and a try-it prompt. Scenarios test judgment under realistic pressure. Labs prove you can execute. The mock assessment ties it all together.
Knowledge checks verify understanding before a lesson counts complete — you cannot click through. Spaced repetition resurfaces weak areas automatically.
Your progress syncs as you work. A domain is mastered when lessons are verified, scenarios answered, and labs completed.

example.code:
Day 1: complete all 4 Start Here lessons
Day 2-3: first two content domains (lessons + scenarios)
Day 4+: one domain per day, labs each evening
Final 3 days: mock assessment runs + capstone build
example.walkthrough: This order exists because later domains assume earlier vocabulary. Skipping ahead creates gaps that the mock assessment will expose — painfully. Trust the sequence.

pitfalls: Skimming lessons without attempting the knowledge check — verification is the learning, not a gate to dodge.
Doing scenarios before reading the domain lessons — scenarios assume the concepts; you will guess instead of reason.
Ignoring the Terminal labs — hands-on execution is what separates passing from failing on performance-based questions.

lessons.title: Cloud+ / Server+ Exam Strategy
concepts: Cloud+ / Server+ tests applied judgment more than memorization. Roughly a third of questions are scenario-based: read the situation, eliminate distractors, pick the BEST answer — not merely a correct one.
Performance-based questions (PBQs) simulate real tasks: drag-and-drop, CLI output analysis, log reading. The labs in this bootcamp are PBQ rehearsal — treat every lab as exam practice.
Time budget: divide total minutes by question count before you start, then check the clock every 20 questions. Flag hard questions and move on — a stuck minute is a lost minute.
Elimination first: cross out the two obviously wrong choices, then compare the remaining two against the question's constraints (cheapest? most secure? first step?).
Never leave a question blank. There is no penalty for wrong answers — an educated guess beats an empty one every time.

example.code:
Q: 'A user reports... Which should you do FIRST?'
  → The word FIRST is the whole question.
  → Eliminate any choice that is a later step.
  → Among the rest, pick the diagnostic before the fix.
example.walkthrough: Exam writers love FIRST, BEST, MOST, and LEAST. Those words change the answer even when the scenario looks identical. Read the actual question stem twice — once for the story, once for the ask.

pitfalls: Answering the scenario instead of the question — the story is context; the final sentence is the task.
Changing answers on review without new evidence — first instincts outperform second-guessing statistically.
Memorizing acronyms without understanding the process behind them — PBQs punish surface knowledge.
lessons.try_it: Take any scenario in this bootcamp, cover the choices, and write what the question is really asking in one sentence before looking at options.

lessons.title: Study System: Spaced Repetition That Sticks
concepts: Forgetting is the default — plan for it. Review a domain's key concepts at expanding intervals: 1 day, 3 days, 7 days, 14 days. Each successful recall strengthens the memory trace.
Active recall beats re-reading: close the lesson and explain the concept aloud in your own words. If you cannot explain it, you do not know it yet.
Interleave domains instead of block-studying one: mix scenarios from two domains in a session. Exams mix topics — your practice should too.
The Feynman check: after each lesson, write a 3-sentence explanation a junior could follow. Vague sentences reveal vague understanding.
Weekly rhythm: 2 domains + 1 hands-on lab per week; mock at week 4 and 6.

example.code:
Session template (90 min):
  0-10   warm-up: 5 flashcards / quick recalls
  10-50  new domain: lessons + knowledge checks
  50-75  scenarios from today + one older domain (interleaving)
  75-90  one terminal lab, then 3-sentence Feynman writes
example.walkthrough: Ninety focused minutes beat four distracted hours. The template above is engineered for retention, not seat time — protect the lab block, it is where skills become reflexes.

pitfalls: Re-reading notes and calling it studying — recognition is not recall; the exam tests recall.
Cramming new domains the night before — sleep consolidates memory; an all-nighter trades retention for exhaustion.
Skipping the Feynman write — it feels slow, but it is the fastest diagnostic of real understanding.

lessons.title: Systems Thinking: Your Unfair Advantage
concepts: Exams and interviews reward systems thinkers: people who trace a request end-to-end instead of reciting isolated facts. This bootcamp trains that explicitly in the Systems Anatomy domain.
The four-step method: (1) see the whole in context, (2) cut it open to reveal layers, (3) walk the process step-by-step, (4) pull apart into labeled pieces.
Every troubleshooting scenario here is a systems trace in disguise: start from the symptom, walk backward through dependencies, find where the expected flow diverges from reality.
In interviews, narrate the journey: 'the request starts here, then…' — hiring managers hear senior-level thinking when you trace instead of define.
The Systems Anatomy explorer in Visuals lets you step through living systems click by click. Use it before each domain's scenarios.

example.code:
Weak answer: 'DNS resolves names to IPs.'
Strong answer: 'The stub resolver asks the recursive resolver, which walks root → TLD → authoritative, caching at each level — that is why the first lookup is slow and the second is instant.'
example.walkthrough: One narrated journey demonstrates more competence than ten memorized definitions. Practice this voice in every scenario's 'why' explanation — read them aloud.

pitfalls: Defining terms instead of tracing flows when asked 'how does X work?'
Jumping to fixes before mapping the system — fixes applied to the wrong layer waste time and credibility.
Treating each domain as separate — the mock assessment deliberately chains them; practice connecting domains now.

lessons.title: Mock Assessment Briefing: Rules of Engagement
concepts: The mock simulates Cloud+ / Server+ conditions: timed, mixed-domain, no hints, one shot per question. Treat it as the real exam — same chair, same focus, no phone.
Scoring mirrors the real exam's weighting: scenario judgment counts more than recall. A wrong answer on a multi-step scenario costs more than a missed definition.
Run the mock only after all domains show 80%+ mastery. Running it early wastes its diagnostic value — it is a measuring instrument, not a study tool.
After each run, the review breaks down misses by domain. Your next study block targets exactly those domains — the mock tells you where to aim.
Two full runs minimum: the first finds gaps, the second confirms they are closed. A passing second run is your green light.

example.code:
Mock protocol:
  1. Silence notifications, full-screen the bootcamp
  2. Note start time; budget per-question time on paper
  3. Answer every question — no blanks
  4. Flag-and-move on stuck questions; return with fresh eyes
  5. Review the domain breakdown before any celebration
example.walkthrough: The mock's value is the breakdown, not the score. A 68% with a clear miss-map beats a lucky 82% — the map tells you exactly what to study next.

pitfalls: Peeking at notes mid-mock — it inflates the score and destroys the diagnostic.
Running the mock as a first activity — without domain mastery it only measures unpreparedness.
Ignoring the domain breakdown — the score is trivia; the miss-map is the study plan.
lessons.try_it: Check your domain mastery percentages now. List any domain under 80% — those are your pre-mock targets.

lessons.title: Reviewing a Mock Run: Turning Misses into Mastery
concepts: For every missed question, classify the error: knowledge gap (never learned it), application gap (knew it, misapplied it), or reading error (misread the ask). Each type needs a different fix.
Knowledge gaps go back to the domain lesson — re-read, re-verify, Feynman-write. Application gaps need more scenarios, not more reading. Reading errors need the exam-strategy lesson again.
Keep an error log: question topic, error type, correct reasoning in one sentence. Patterns emerge fast — three 'reading errors' in a row is a process problem, not a knowledge problem.
Re-test missed topics within 48 hours with fresh scenarios. A corrected mistake that is not re-tested is a mistake waiting to recur.
Your second mock run should show misses migrating: fewer knowledge gaps, zero repeated reading errors. That migration is the signal you are ready.

example.code:
Error log entry:
  Q: firewall rule order scenario → chose 'deny' before 'allow'
  Type: application gap (knew rule order, misapplied under time pressure)
  Fix: 5 more firewall scenarios, timed
  Correct reasoning: 'First match wins — the allow had to precede the deny.'
example.walkthrough: Do not just re-read the explanation and move on. The error log forces you to name the failure mode — and named failures are fixable failures.

pitfalls: Re-reading explanations passively — recognition feels like learning but evaporates under pressure.
Studying only the missed topics and neglecting maintenance review of strong ones — strengths decay too.
Taking the second mock too soon — give fixes 48 hours and a re-test cycle first.
lessons.try_it: Create your error log file now (paper or notes app). You will need it after your first mock run.

lessons.title: Capstone Plan: What You Will Build and Why
concepts: Employers and examiners trust demonstrated skill over claimed knowledge. Your capstone is a working artifact — something you can screenshare and narrate in under 10 minutes.
Pick ONE project from the list below. Depth beats breadth: a single polished build outperforms three half-finished ones.
Scope it to finish in 2–3 focused sessions. If it needs more, cut features — a complete small project beats an ambitious pile of parts.
Document as you go: every decision gets a one-line reason. That log becomes your interview narration script.
Done means: it works end-to-end, you can demo it live, and you can explain every part without notes.

example.code:
Pick your project:
  1. Hybrid Lab Environment — virtualized servers + cloud resources with IaC
  2. Monitoring Stack — metrics, logs, and alerting for a lab infrastructure
  3. Backup & Restore Drill — documented 3-2-1 backup with tested restores
example.walkthrough: Choose the project that scares you slightly — that is where the growth is. But cap the scope ruthlessly: you must finish.

pitfalls: Starting two projects and finishing neither — pick one, finish it, then consider a second.
Building without documenting — the demo narration is half the value; no log means no story.
Gold-plating instead of finishing — ship the working core first, polish only if time remains.

lessons.title: Build Log: Decisions, Dead Ends, and Proof
concepts: Keep a build log with timestamps: what you tried, what happened, what you changed. Dead ends are valuable — they prove you debugged, not just followed a tutorial.
For each component, record: purpose (one line), how it works (three lines), how you tested it (one command or check).
Screenshot or record key milestones. A 60-second screen recording of the working project is worth more than a page of description.
Version your work: even a simple dated folder structure beats a single 'final' file. Show the progression.
The log is not overhead — it IS the deliverable's companion. Interviewers ask 'tell me about a challenge'; your log hands you the answer.

example.code:
Build log entry:
  14:32 — Tried X config; service failed with error Y
  14:47 — Found cause: Z was misconfigured (docs said A, reality was B)
  15:05 — Fixed; verified with [test command]; works end-to-end
example.walkthrough: Write the log as you go, not after. Memory lies; timestamps do not. Future-you (in the interview) will thank present-you.

pitfalls: Writing the log from memory at the end — you will forget the dead ends, which are the best stories.
Skipping the 'how I tested it' line — untested claims collapse under the first interview question.
No recordings — a live demo can fail; a recording is bulletproof backup.

lessons.title: Demo Day: Narrating Your Build in 10 Minutes
concepts: Structure the demo: problem (1 min) → architecture (2 min) → live walkthrough (5 min) → lessons learned (2 min). Rehearse it twice, timed.
Narrate the systems journey: 'a request starts here, flows through…' — the Systems Anatomy voice. Show you understand the whole, not just the parts you typed.
Prepare for three hard questions: 'why this approach over X?', 'what breaks at scale?', 'what would you do differently?'. Write your answers in advance.
Lead with the working demo, not slides. Working software presented live beats any deck.
End with the repo/README link and offer to walk through the code. Make it effortless for them to verify your work.

example.code:
Demo script skeleton:
  'I built [X] because [problem]. It works by [3-step journey].
   Watch: [live action]. The tricky part was [challenge] —
   I solved it by [approach]. Code and docs are at [link].'
example.walkthrough: Rehearsal is non-negotiable. A polished 10-minute demo signals preparation, communication skill, and genuine ownership — exactly what hiring managers screen for.

pitfalls: Wing the demo — 'let me just show you' without a plan wastes the moment.
Hiding the challenges — the dead ends and fixes are what prove real engineering happened.
No backup plan — have the recording ready in case live demo gods are unkind.
lessons.try_it: Draft your three hard-question answers now, before you build. They will sharpen your design decisions.

lessons.title: Roles That Hire CompTIA Infrastructure (Cloud+/Server+) Skills
concepts: The roles: Systems Administrator, Cloud Engineer, Infrastructure Engineer, DevOps Engineer. Read 10 job postings and extract the repeated requirements — that list is your real syllabus.
Titles vary by company; skills cluster by function. Map postings to skill clusters (not titles) to see what the market actually buys.
Entry points differ: some roles hire on certification + projects, others on portfolio + interviews. Know your target's gate before optimizing for it.
Salary bands follow scarcity + impact: specialized + revenue-adjacent pays more. Position yourself at that intersection deliberately.
Track the market quarterly: which skills are rising in postings? Your learning backlog should follow the demand signal.

  My gaps: ___ → study priority

Ignoring the 'repeated requirements' — what 8/10 postings demand is the real bar.
No gap analysis — studying without knowing your gaps is motion without direction.

lessons.title: Resume & Projects That Get Callbacks
concepts: Resumes get 30 seconds: lead with a skills line matching the posting's keywords, then 3-4 bullets per role with quantified outcomes (not duties).
Projects beat buzzwords: one deployed, documented project outweighs a paragraph of claimed skills. Link the repo AND the live demo.
Tailor per application: mirror the posting's language for the top 5 requirements. ATS filters are literal — 'PostgreSQL' does not match 'postgres' in dumb parsers.
The capstone in this bootcamp IS your resume project: finish it, document it, link it. That single line does more work than any certification bullet.
GitHub profile hygiene: pinned repos with READMEs, green contribution squares, no empty forks. Recruiters do click through.

  Weak: 'Responsible for databases.'
  Strong: 'Migrated 2TB analytics DB to Postgres; cut query p95 40%; zero-downtime cutover.'
example.walkthrough: Every bullet must answer: what did you do, at what scale, to what effect? Duties describe jobs; outcomes get interviews.

pitfalls: Skill lists without evidence — every claimed skill needs a project or role bullet backing it.
One generic resume for all applications — tailoring is the highest-ROI 20 minutes in job hunting.
No links — a project without a URL might as well not exist.
