lessons.title: Interview Loops: What Actually Happens
concepts: Typical loop: recruiter screen (15 min, fit + comp) → technical screen (45-60 min, live problems) → onsite/virtual loop (3-5 rounds: technical depth, system design, behavioral) → offer.
Technical screens test thinking aloud: narrate your approach before coding/querying. Silence is scored as stuck; structured thinking is scored as senior.
Behavioral rounds use STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) — prepare 5 stories covering: conflict, failure, leadership, ambiguity, and impact. Quantify results.
Questions YOU ask matter: 'what does success look like in 90 days?' and 'what's the hardest problem the team faces?' signal seriousness. Never ask nothing.
Follow up within 24 hours: thank-you note referencing something specific from the conversation. Small effort, real signal.

example.code:
STAR story skeleton:
  S: 'Our deploy pipeline broke weekly...'
  T: 'I owned stabilizing it in Q3...'
  A: 'I added staged rollouts + runbook...'
  R: 'Deploys went from 60% to 99% success; on-call pages dropped 70%.'
example.walkthrough: Prepare stories, not scripts: know your 5 STAR stories cold enough to adapt to any behavioral question. Rehearse aloud twice.

pitfalls: No questions for them — reads as disinterest; always ask two.
Rambling technical answers — structure: approach first, then detail, then verify.
Badmouthing past employers — the interviewer hears how you will talk about THEM.
lessons.try_it: Draft one STAR story now using the skeleton. Time it — aim for 90 seconds.

lessons.title: The CompTIA Infrastructure (Cloud+/Server+) Tool Landscape
concepts: Tools cluster by job-to-be-done, not by vendor. Learn the categories first, then pick one tool per category deeply — depth in one beats surface in five.
The 80/20 rule: 20% of each tool's features cover 80% of real work. Master the core workflow before exploring the edges.
Free/open tiers are enough to learn: every major platform has a free tier or community edition sufficient for portfolio projects. Never pay to learn the basics.
Tool churn is constant; fundamentals are stable. SQL outlives every BI tool; TCP/IP outlives every cloud console. Invest in fundamentals first.

For CompTIA Infrastructure (Cloud+/Server+), the essential categories:
  Virtualization: Proxmox/VMware
  Cloud: AWS/Azure free tier
  IaC: Terraform/Ansible
  Monitoring: Prometheus/Grafana

example.code:
Learning order:
  1. One tool per category, core workflow only
  2. Build the capstone using exactly these tools
  3. Add a second tool per category only when a job posting demands it
example.walkthrough: Resist tool tourism: each new tool costs weeks. The portfolio proves depth; the resume lists breadth honestly.

pitfalls: Learning 5 tools shallowly instead of 2 deeply — interviews probe depth.
Paying for premium tiers to learn — free tiers cover 90% of learning needs.
Chasing every new release — fundamentals first; novelty second.
lessons.try_it: List your one-tool-per-category stack now. Identify any category where you have zero depth — that is your next lab.

lessons.title: Workflows: Connecting the Tools
concepts: Tools in isolation are trivia; workflows are skill. The professional unit is the end-to-end flow: ingest → transform → validate → deliver — across YOUR tool stack.
Document your workflows as runbooks: trigger, steps, verification, rollback. A runbook turns personal knowledge into team capability.
Automate the toil, not the judgment: repetitive steps get scripted; decisions stay human. If you do it weekly, automate it.
Version everything: code, configs, queries, dashboards. 'Final_v2_ACTUAL' is not version control — git is.
The workflow IS the portfolio piece: 'here is my pipeline, here is the runbook, here is the monitoring' — that sentence hires.

example.code:
Runbook skeleton:
  Trigger: ___ (schedule/event/manual)
  Steps: 1.___ 2.___ 3.___
  Verify: ___ (how do you know it worked?)
  Rollback: ___ (how do you undo it?)
  Owner: ___  Last tested: ___
example.walkthrough: Write the runbook BEFORE automating: it forces you to understand the workflow well enough to hand it to someone else.

pitfalls: Automating before documenting — you encode confusion at machine speed.
No verification step — a workflow without a check is a hope with extra steps.
No rollback plan — the first failure without one teaches this lesson permanently.
lessons.try_it: Write a runbook for one workflow you do regularly, using the skeleton above.

lessons.title: Cloud+ PBQ Patterns
concepts: Infrastructure PBQs simulate: analyzing `df -h` / `free -m` output to diagnose resource exhaustion, matching VM sizes to workload requirements, ordering deployment steps, reading cloud cost reports.

For resource-output PBQs: check the USE% column first — the resource at 95%+ is the story. Then match the symptom to the bottleneck (swap thrashing = memory, iowait = storage, load without CPU = I/O wait).
For sizing PBQs: gather requirements (vCPU, RAM, IOPS, network) then pick the SMALLEST instance/VM that meets all four — oversizing wastes budget and is a wrong answer.
For ordering PBQs (deployments, migrations): dependencies first — network before compute, storage before database, identity before access. Draw the dependency arrow mentally.
Linux+ crossover: know `systemctl`, `journalctl`, permissions, and LVM basics. The exams share DNA — one study effort feeds both.

example.code:
PBQ: 'The VM is slow. Diagnose from the output.'
  free -m: Mem 8192 total, 7900 used, swap 2048 used 1900
  top: %wa (iowait) 45%
  Diagnosis: memory exhausted → swapping → disk thrash.
  Fix: add RAM (or find the leak) — not faster disks.
example.walkthrough: Read output like a doctor reads labs: the abnormal value names the disease. Train on real command output, not descriptions of it.

pitfalls: Adding CPU to a memory-starved VM — the bottleneck names the fix; more of the wrong resource changes nothing.
Rebooting as diagnosis — it clears symptoms and destroys evidence; read the output first.
Choosing the biggest instance 'to be safe' — exams penalize waste; right-size to requirements.
lessons.try_it: Run `free -m` and `df -h` on any Linux system now. Identify the tightest resource and state the fix in one sentence.

lessons.title: Right-Sizing Compute & Memory
concepts: Capacity planning answers: how much do we need, when will we run out, and what does growth cost? Every answer needs a measurement, a trend, and a headroom policy.
Measure first: 30 days of CPU, memory, disk IOPS, and network throughput at 5-minute granularity. Averages lie — plan against the 95th percentile, not the mean.
Headroom policy: 70% sustained utilization is the planning ceiling for most workloads. Above it, performance degrades and burst capacity vanishes. Budget for headroom explicitly.
Memory sizing: working set + OS overhead + 20% headroom. For VMs, right-size the guest first — oversized guests waste host memory through ballooning and idle pages.
vCPU sizing: start 1:1 with measured need, monitor ready-time (VMware) or steal-time (KVM). Ready-time above 5% means the host is overcommitted — add hosts or reduce vCPUs.

example.code:
Web tier: 95th-pct CPU 55% on 4 vCPU, memory 6GB of 8GB used.
  Verdict: healthy — under the 70% ceiling with headroom.
  DB tier: 95th-pct CPU 82%, memory 15GB of 16GB, swap active.
  Verdict: undersized — add RAM first (swap is the smoking gun), then evaluate CPU.
example.walkthrough: Undersizing causes outages; oversizing causes budget reviews. The 95th percentile plus a headroom policy is the professional middle.

pitfalls: Planning against averages — the 95th percentile is where outages live.
Ignoring swap activity — any sustained swap means memory is undersized, full stop.
Sizing for today with no growth factor — get the growth rate in writing from the business.
lessons.try_it: Write the 4-line capacity statement for a workload you know: measurement, 95th pct, headroom status, recommendation.

lessons.title: Storage Sizing: IOPS, Throughput, Capacity
concepts: Storage has three axes: capacity (how much), IOPS (how many operations), throughput (how many bytes/sec). Workloads bottleneck on different axes — databases on IOPS, video on throughput, archives on capacity.

RAID math: RAID 10 gives ~50% usable capacity with the best write performance; RAID 5 gives (n-1)/n usable but suffers write penalty (4 I/Os per write); RAID 6 tolerates 2 disk failures at (n-2)/n usable.
IOPS planning: measure current IOPS at peak, add growth, then verify the array's rated IOPS exceed it with headroom. SSDs deliver 10–100x the IOPS of HDDs — tier accordingly.
Do not forget the network path: 10GbE iSCSI can bottleneck before the array does. End-to-end thinking — array, fabric, host — or the fastest disk in the world waits on a slow wire.
Cloud storage tiers map to access patterns: hot (frequent), cool (monthly), archive (yearly). Mis-tiering is the #1 cloud storage cost leak — lifecycle policies automate it.

example.code:
DB needs 8TB usable, 5000 IOPS, tolerates 1 disk failure:
  RAID 10: 16TB raw → 8TB usable, best IOPS — pick this for write-heavy DB
  RAID 5: ~10TB raw → 8TB usable, write penalty hurts DB
  Verdict: RAID 10 on SSD; verify fabric ≥ 16Gb/s end-to-end.
example.walkthrough: Size all three axes or the one you skipped becomes the outage. The RAID decision is a trade-off table, not a habit — write the table.

pitfalls: Sizing only capacity — the array holds the data but cannot serve it fast enough.
RAID 5 for write-heavy databases — the write penalty compounds under load.
Forgetting the fabric — array IOPS mean nothing if the HBA or network caps throughput.
lessons.try_it: Build the RAID trade-off table (usable %, fault tolerance, write penalty, best use) for RAID 0/1/5/6/10 from memory.

lessons.title: Identity Across the Hybrid Boundary
concepts: Hybrid identity starts with one truth: users exist once. Entra Connect / AD sync makes on-prem AD the source and cloud the replica — or go cloud-native with federation. Pick one model deliberately.

SSO across the boundary needs federation (SAML/OIDC) or seamless SSO: the user authenticates once on-prem and the token is honored in cloud. Password hash sync is the simplest; pass-through keeps auth on-prem.
Conditional Access must span both worlds: require MFA for cloud apps AND on-prem resources, device compliance everywhere. A policy that covers only cloud is a policy with a hole.
The network seam: ExpressRoute/Direct Connect (private, SLA) vs site-to-site VPN (encrypted, internet). Private is not automatically trusted — encrypt and authenticate regardless.
DNS is the invisible seam: on-prem names must resolve in cloud and vice versa. Split-brain or conditional forwarders — decide, document, monitor. Half the 'hybrid is broken' tickets are DNS.

example.code:
User opens cloud app from office:
  1. Redirect to on-prem ADFS (federation) → Kerberos SSO, no password
  2. Token issued, presented to cloud app → access granted
  3. Conditional Access evaluated: compliant device? → yes → allow
  Break any link — expired cert, DNS failure, revoked trust — and SSO dies silently.
example.walkthrough: Hybrid is two systems pretending to be one. The seams — identity, network, DNS — are where outages live. Map every seam explicitly.

pitfalls: Two identity sources with no sync authority — which one is truth? Decide before the first sync.
Assuming ExpressRoute needs no encryption — private transport is not trusted transport.
Forgetting DNS in the hybrid design — name resolution across the seam breaks everything quietly.
lessons.try_it: Draw your hybrid identity flow: user → auth → token → app, labeling the trust at each arrow.

lessons.title: Data Flow in Hybrid: Where Does It Live?
concepts: Data gravity decides architecture: large datasets stay where they are analyzed. Moving terabytes to the cloud for one query is the expensive mistake — bring compute to data when gravity is strong.

Classify before you migrate: hot data (daily use) near compute, warm data (monthly) in cheap object storage, cold data (compliance) in archive tier. Unclassified data gets the expensive tier by default.
Egress charges are the hidden bill: ingress is usually free, egress is metered. Architectures that chat across the boundary (chatty APIs, uncompressed replication) bleed money.

Backup across the boundary needs the 3-2-1 rule reinterpreted: 3 copies, 2 media types, 1 offsite — where 'offsite' can be the other side of the hybrid seam. Test restores across the seam, not just within it.
Sovereignty and compliance may forbid the seam entirely for some datasets: know which data cannot leave the building before designing the flow.

example.code:
10TB analytics dataset, queried daily by on-prem BI:
  Bad: copy 10TB to cloud nightly ($$$ egress + time)
  Good: cloud compute queries via private link, results (MBs) return
  Better: keep hot data on-prem, archive cold partitions to cloud tier
example.walkthrough: Follow the bytes and the dollars together. Every cross-seam flow has a latency cost AND a meter running — design for both.

pitfalls: Migrating data before classifying it — the archive tier exists; use it.
Ignoring egress in the TCO — the cloud bill surprise is always egress.
Untested cross-seam restores — a backup you cannot restore across the boundary is not a backup.
lessons.try_it: Trace one data flow you know across a boundary (any boundary). Label bytes moved, frequency, and cost per crossing.

lessons.title: From Clicking to Code: First IaC Steps
concepts: Infrastructure as Code means the environment is defined in versioned text files, not in someone's memory of console clicks. If it is not in code, it does not exist — it is folklore.
Start with the boring wins: VM templates, network configs, user accounts. Automate what you do monthly before what you do yearly — frequency justifies the investment.

Declarative (Terraform, ARM/Bicep, CloudFormation) states the desired end — the tool figures out the steps. Imperative (scripts) lists the steps. Declarative wins for infrastructure; imperative for one-off tasks.
State is the hard part: Terraform state files, Ansible idempotency. The tool must know what exists to compute what must change. Protect state like production data — because it is.
Test the code, not just the result: `terraform plan` before `apply`, lint templates in CI, and keep a non-production environment where `apply` runs first.

example.code:
Manual: click 47 times to build a VM → works once, undocumented, unrepeatable
  IaC: terraform apply → identical VM in 4 minutes, code-reviewed, repeatable 100x
  The second VM costs the same 4 minutes. The manual second VM costs another 47 clicks + drift.
example.walkthrough: The question is not 'can I automate this' but 'how many times will I do this before automation pays off' — usually the answer is three.

pitfalls: Automating a broken process — code makes bad process faster, not better; fix the process first.
No state protection — a deleted state file turns managed infrastructure into mystery meat.
Applying to production first — plan, then staging, then production. The order is the safety.
lessons.try_it: Pick one monthly manual task you do. Write the 5-line pseudo-plan: trigger, desired state, verification, rollback.

lessons.title: Configuration Management Discipline
concepts: Configuration drift is entropy: servers slowly diverge from their intended state through hotfixes and manual tweaks. Config management (Ansible, DSC, Chef) continuously enforces the declared state.
Idempotency is the core property: running the playbook twice produces the same result as running it once. Every task must be safe to re-run — check-then-act, never blind-act.

Roles and playbooks are documentation that executes: the Ansible role for 'web server' IS the build doc. If the doc and the role disagree, the role wins — so keep them in sync by generating docs from code.
Secrets do not belong in playbooks: use a vault (Ansible Vault at minimum, HSM/KMS-backed for production). A secret in git is a secret compromised — rotate it the moment it lands in version control.
Run in check mode first, limit blast radius with batches, and keep the last-known-good playbook tagged. Automation at scale needs the same change discipline as code deploys.

example.code:
Playbook: ensure NTP configured on all web servers
  Task: template ntp.conf → notify restart ntpd (handler, only on change)
  Run 1: 40 hosts changed. Run 2: 0 hosts changed — idempotent.
  Host 41 added later → next run configures only host 41.
example.walkthrough: Idempotency turns 'run it and hope' into 'run it and know'. If your automation is not safe to run twice, it is not automation — it is a script with ambitions.

pitfalls: Non-idempotent tasks (append without check) — run twice, get duplicates; run ten times, get a mess.
Secrets in plaintext in the repo — assume compromise and rotate; then vault them properly.
No check mode / no batching — a typo should not reconfigure the entire fleet at once.
lessons.try_it: Write a 3-task idempotent playbook on paper: install package X, ensure service Y running, deploy config Z. Mark each task's idempotency mechanism.

lessons.title: Test-Day Protocol: The Final 24 Hours
concepts: No new material: review command cheat sheets, the PBQ patterns, and exam strategy only.
Logistics: ID, confirmation, route. Arrive early; breathe.
Sleep 8 hours. Command syntax recall needs a rested brain.
During: read PBQ tasks twice, smallest verifiable step first, flag-and-move.

example.code: T-24h: [ ] command flashcards [ ] ID + route [ ] 8h sleep [ ] PBQ protocol
example.walkthrough: Trust the labs. You have executed these commands — the exam just asks you to recognize them.

pitfalls: Cramming new commands.
All-nighter.
Skipping logistics.
lessons.try_it: Run through your 10 most-used commands from memory. Any hesitation = flashcard it.

lessons.title: Forecasting Growth
concepts: Forecasting needs history: 6-12 months of utilization data minimum. Less than that and you are guessing with extra steps — say so honestly.
Linear trend + seasonality: most infrastructure grows linearly with seasonal bumps. Fit the trend, note the peaks, plan for peak + headroom — not the average.
Event-driven growth breaks trends: product launches, acquisitions, viral moments. Keep a 20% buffer for the unplannable — and a fast procurement path.
Present forecasts as ranges: 'we need 40-60TB by Q3, most likely 48TB.' Ranges are honest; point estimates are lies with decimal places.
Review quarterly: forecasts decay. The Q1 forecast is stale by Q3 — refresh it on a cadence, not when panic strikes.

example.code:
Storage forecast:
  Current: 30TB, growing 1.5TB/quarter (linear, R²=0.94)
  Q3 need: 30 + 3×1.5 = 34.5TB → plan 40TB (headroom)
  Range: 37-43TB. Procure at 35TB used (lead time!).
  Honest, ranged, actionable.
example.walkthrough: Forecasting is applied humility: the range matters more than the point, and the review cadence matters more than the model.

pitfalls: Point-estimate forecasts — false precision; always present ranges.
Ignoring lead times — procurement takes weeks; trigger orders BEFORE need.
Set-and-forget forecasts — refresh quarterly or the forecast becomes fiction.
lessons.try_it: Forecast one resource you manage: 4 quarters of history, trend, range for next 2 quarters.

lessons.title: Migration Strategies: 6 Rs
concepts: The 6 Rs: Rehost (lift-and-shift), Replatform (minor tweaks), Repurchase (SaaS swap), Refactor (re-architect), Retain (stay), Retire (decommission). Name the strategy per workload — no defaults.
Rehost is fastest but imports technical debt to the cloud (and the bill). Use for time pressure; plan the refactor as phase 2 — or the debt compounds.
Retire first: 20-30% of discovered workloads are unused. Decommission before migrating — the cheapest migration is the one you don't do.
Wave planning: start with low-risk, low-dependency workloads (dev/test). Learn the process cheaply, then attack the critical systems with experience.
Rollback per wave: each migration needs a backout plan tested BEFORE cutover. 'We'll figure it out' is not a rollback plan.

example.code:
Wave 1 (learn): dev/test environments — rehost, low risk.
  Wave 2 (prove): internal apps — replatform to managed DB.
  Wave 3 (earn): customer-facing — refactor critical paths.
  Throughout: retire the 25% nobody uses. Discovered, not migrated.
example.walkthrough: Migration is a portfolio exercise: each workload gets its own R, its own wave, its own rollback. The plan is the project.

pitfalls: Lift-and-shift everything — imports debt and maximizes the bill.
No retirement pass — migrating dead workloads is expensive theater.
Big-bang cutover — waves exist because big bangs create big outages.
lessons.try_it: Classify 5 workloads you know into the 6 Rs. Which wave goes first? Why?

lessons.title: GitOps for Infrastructure
concepts: GitOps: git is the source of truth; agents reconcile reality to git. Change = pull request; deploy = merge. The audit trail is free — it is the git log.
The loop: PR → review → CI validates (plan/lint) → merge → agent applies → drift detection alerts on manual changes. Every step is visible and reversible.
Drift detection is the killer feature: manual console changes get flagged (or auto-reverted). The 'quick fix in the console' dies — and good riddance.
Secrets in GitOps: sealed secrets or external vault references — never plaintext. The repo is the truth, but some truths are encrypted.
Start small: one non-critical service, full GitOps loop. Prove the workflow, then expand. The cultural shift (no more console cowboys) is the hard part.

example.code:
GitOps loop:
  1. Edit infra/values.yaml → PR
  2. CI: terraform plan posted as comment
  3. Review + merge
  4. Agent applies; dashboard shows sync
  5. Manual console change → drift alert in 5 min
  Every change reviewed, tested, traceable.
example.walkthrough: GitOps turns infrastructure into software engineering: reviewed, tested, reversible. The console becomes read-only by culture.

pitfalls: Plaintext secrets in git — sealed/vault references only; the repo is public to the team.
No drift detection — without it, GitOps is just 'git-stored' with extra steps.
Big-bang adoption — one service first; the workflow must prove itself.
lessons.try_it: Sketch the GitOps loop for one service you manage. What breaks first in your current process?

lessons.title: Designing for Failure: HA Patterns
concepts: High availability is math: two components at 99% each in parallel ≈ 99.99% together. Design with redundancy at every tier — no single points of failure in the critical path.
AZ/region spread: single-AZ is a gamble; multi-AZ survives datacenter failure; multi-region survives regional failure. Each level costs more — match to the SLA the business actually needs.
Load balancer health checks define 'healthy': check the real dependency (can the app reach its DB?), not just TCP-open. Shallow checks route traffic to broken backends.
Stateless app tier + shared state (DB, object storage, cache): the pattern that scales horizontally. Session state on local disk is the scaling killer — externalize it.
Test the failure, not just the design: chaos drills (kill an AZ, fail the primary DB) prove HA works. Untested HA is a hope with architecture diagrams.

example.code:
3-tier HA:
  ALB (multi-AZ) → app servers (2+ AZs, stateless, auto-scaling)
    → RDS Multi-AZ (sync standby) → S3 (11 nines)
  Kill AZ-a: ALB drains, ASG replaces, RDS fails over.
  RTO minutes, RPO seconds — if tested. Untested: unknown.
example.walkthrough: Design for the failure you fear, then TEST that failure. The drill is the architecture's proof.

pitfalls: Single-AZ 'HA' — one datacenter event ends the story.
Health checks on '/' only — the app serves 200 while the DB is down; check dependencies.
Stateful app servers — sticky sessions + local state = unscalable and fragile.
lessons.try_it: Draw your (real or lab) app's HA design. Circle every single point of failure. How many?

lessons.title: Cost Control in the Cloud
concepts: The cloud bill is an architecture review in disguise: every line item maps to a design decision. Tag everything (owner, project, environment) or the bill is unactionable.
Right-size continuously: cloud makes resizing cheap, so oversizing is a choice — review instance sizes quarterly against actual utilization.
Commitment discounts (reserved/savings plans) for steady-state workloads: 30-70% off for a 1-3 year commitment. Only commit to the baseline you KNOW is stable.
Storage lifecycle policies automate tiering: hot → cool after 30 days → archive after 90. Unmanaged storage grows forever at the expensive tier.
Kill the zombies: unattached disks, idle load balancers, old snapshots, forgotten dev instances. A monthly 'zombie hunt' typically finds 10-20% waste.

example.code:
Monthly bill $12k → zombie hunt finds:
  Unattached EBS: $800/mo — delete (snapshot first)
  Idle LB: $200/mo — delete
  Oversized RDS (5% CPU): $1,500 → downsize saves $900
  No lifecycle on logs bucket: $600/mo → policy saves $450
  Total found: ~$2,350/mo (20%) in one afternoon.
example.walkthrough: Treat cloud spend as an engineering metric: dashboard it, alert on anomalies, review monthly. FinOps is not finance's job — it is architecture's.

pitfalls: No tagging — the bill arrives as a lump; nobody owns it.
Reserved instances for spiky workloads — commitments need stable baselines.
Ignoring storage growth — logs and snapshots compound silently; lifecycle policies are the fix.
lessons.try_it: List 5 zombie-hunt checks for your cloud account. Run them (or simulate) and total the waste.

lessons.title: Users, Groups, and sudo Done Right
concepts: Every human gets a unique account: shared accounts destroy accountability. Service accounts get no login shell and minimal rights — they are not people.
sudo, not root login: `visudo` for syntax-checked edits, per-command sudoers entries for service accounts, and full logging of sudo use. Root password in a vault, rarely used.
Groups express roles: `developers`, `dbadmins`, `deploy` — permissions attach to groups, users join groups. Never permission individuals directly; the join/leave IS the access review.
SSH keys over passwords: key-only auth, no root login, non-standard port optional (obscurity ≠ security, but it cuts log noise). ssh-agent, not password typing.
Offboard in one command: userdel + remove from groups + revoke keys + kill sessions. Write the script BEFORE you need it at 5pm on a Friday.

example.code:
Onboarding:
  useradd -m -G developers -s /bin/bash alice
  mkdir -p /home/alice/.ssh && cat key.pub >> authorized_keys
  chmod 700 .ssh && chmod 600 authorized_keys
  Test: ssh alice@host (key only, no password prompt)
  Offboard: reverse it all, one script.
example.walkthrough: Identity is the first control: unique accounts, key auth, group-based rights, scripted lifecycle. Get this right and half of Linux security follows.

pitfalls: Shared 'admin' accounts — no accountability; every action is anonymous.
Password auth on internet-facing SSH — brute-force bait; keys only.
Manual offboarding — forgotten accounts are attacker accounts; script it.
lessons.try_it: Audit one system: list human users, check for shared accounts, verify no password-auth SSH. Report findings.

lessons.title: Logs: The System's Diary
concepts: journalctl is the modern interface: `journalctl -u nginx --since '1 hour ago'`, `-f` to follow, `-p err` for errors. Learn these three invocations cold.
Log rotation (logrotate) prevents disk-full deaths: size/time-based rotation, compression, retention counts. Unrotated logs are a slow-motion outage.
Centralize: rsyslog/syslog-ng forwarding to a log server, or journal upload. Local-only logs die with the host — exactly when you need them most.
What to log: auth events, sudo use, service restarts, errors. What NOT to log: passwords, tokens, full PII in debug. Log review is a security control; log content is a liability.
Alert on patterns, not just errors: 5 failed SSH logins in a minute, disk at 85%, service restart loops. Thresholds turn logs from archaeology into early warning.

example.code:
Diagnosis via journal:
  systemctl status app → failed
  journalctl -u app --since '30 min ago' → 'bind: address in use'
  ss -tlnp | grep 8080 → old process holding the port
  kill old PID → restart → verified.
  Four commands, five minutes, root cause — logs did the work.
example.walkthrough: When something breaks, the logs already know. The skill is asking them correctly: which unit, what timeframe, what severity.

pitfalls: No rotation — /var/log fills the disk; the outage is self-inflicted.
Local-only logs for critical systems — the evidence burns with the server.
Debug logging in production with secrets — the log file becomes the vulnerability.
lessons.try_it: Check log rotation on your system: `cat /etc/logrotate.conf` + `ls -lh /var/log`. Any unrotated giants?

lessons.title: Package Management Without Fear
concepts: One package manager per system, used consistently: apt (Debian/Ubuntu), dnf (RHEL), never mixed with manual tarball installs in production. Consistency is maintainability.
Update discipline: security updates promptly (unattended-upgrades for security pocket), full upgrades in maintenance windows with snapshots. 'Never update' is how breaches happen.
Pinning/holding for stability: hold kernel or app versions when the business needs stability, but track the held packages — holds expire into technical debt.
Repositories matter: official + vetted third-party (EPEL, vendor repos). Random PPAs and curl-piped-to-bash are supply-chain roulette — verify signatures.
Document the package set: `dpkg --get-selections` / `rpm -qa` baselines, or better, config management declaring packages. Rebuildable servers start with known package lists.

example.code:
Monthly patching:
  1. Snapshot/backup first (rollback exists)
  2. apt update && apt list --upgradable (review!)
  3. Apply security first, then the rest
  4. Reboot if kernel/libs need it (check needrestart)
  5. Verify services; document.
  Boring, regular, safe — that is the goal.
example.walkthrough: Patching is not exciting, which is why it gets skipped — and why unpatched systems dominate breach reports. Make it routine, make it safe, make it happen.

pitfalls: curl | sudo bash — unaudited code as root; the supply-chain nightmare.
Never patching 'because it works' — working and vulnerable is still vulnerable.
No rollback plan — snapshot before, verify after; the order matters.
lessons.try_it: List upgradable packages on your system now. Classify: security vs feature. Would you apply them today?

lessons.title: RAID Revisited: Choosing Wisely
concepts: RAID 0: striping, 100% usable, zero fault tolerance — speed only, never for data you need. RAID 1: mirroring, 50% usable, survives 1 disk — simple and reliable.
RAID 5: (n-1)/n usable, survives 1 disk, write penalty (4 I/Os per write). RAID 6: (n-2)/n usable, survives 2 disks — the safe choice for large SATA arrays where rebuilds take days.
RAID 10: striped mirrors, 50% usable, best performance + good fault tolerance. The database default — pay the capacity cost for the IOPS.
Hot spares vs hot standby: a global hot spare auto-rebuilds on failure; without one, you are degraded until a human intervenes. Always configure the spare.
RAID is not backup: it protects against disk failure, not deletion, corruption, or ransomware. Say it until it is reflex: RAID ≠ backup.

example.code:
8TB usable needed, 8x 2TB disks:
  RAID 5: 14TB usable, 1-disk tolerance, write penalty
  RAID 6: 12TB usable, 2-disk tolerance — safer rebuilds
  RAID 10: 8TB usable exactly, best perf, survives 1/disk-pair
  DB workload → RAID 10. Archive → RAID 6. Never RAID 5 on large disks (rebuild risk).
example.walkthrough: Match RAID to workload: write-heavy → RAID 10; capacity-heavy → RAID 6; and always budget the hot spare.

pitfalls: RAID 5 on 8TB disks — rebuild takes days; second failure during rebuild kills the array.
No hot spare — degraded mode until someone notices; configure the spare.
'We have RAID so we skip backups' — RAID survives disk death, not rm -rf.
lessons.try_it: For a file server (mostly reads, 10TB usable, 6x4TB disks): choose RAID level and justify with math.

lessons.title: Hardware Monitoring and Predictive Failure
concepts: SMART data predicts disk death: reallocated sectors, pending sectors, UDMA CRC errors trending up = replace the drive NOW, not after it dies.
IPMI/iDRAC/iLO is the out-of-band lifeline: power control, console, and sensor data independent of the OS. Configure it before you need it at 2 AM.
Watch the triad: temperatures (CPU, ambient, disk), fans (RPM, failures), power (PSU status, input voltage). Environmental kills hardware silently.
RAID controller battery/flash backup: write-back cache without protection is data loss waiting for a power event. Verify cache protection status quarterly.
Log hardware events centrally: predictive failure alerts should page, not sit in a local log nobody reads. The alert that pages saves the array.

example.code:
Morning check (5 min):
  smartctl -H /dev/sda → PASSED?
  ipmitool sensor list → temps/fans OK?
  RAID status → Optimal? Battery OK?
  Any predictive failures → ticket + replacement ordered TODAY.
example.walkthrough: Hardware fails gradually, then suddenly. The gradual phase is visible in SMART and sensors — if anyone looks. Be the one who looks.

pitfalls: Ignoring SMART warnings — 'still working' is not a maintenance strategy.
No out-of-band management configured — the 2 AM hang needs IPMI, not a drive.
Write-back cache without battery — a power blip becomes data corruption.
lessons.try_it: Run smartctl -H on your disks (or a VM's virtual disk) now. What does it report?

lessons.title: Firmware and Lifecycle Management
concepts: Firmware is software too: BIOS/UEFI, RAID controller, NIC, BMC, and disk firmware all have CVEs. Inventory firmware versions like you inventory OS patches.
Update order: BMC/IPMI first (out-of-band safety), then BIOS/UEFI, then controllers, then disks. Never update all at once without a rollback path.
Lifecycle planning: 3-5 year hardware refresh cycles, warranty alignment, and capacity headroom. Emergency hardware purchases cost 2x planned ones.
Decommission securely: cryptographic erase or physical destruction for disks with sensitive data. A retired server with intact disks is a breach in a dumpster.
Document everything: asset tags, warranty dates, firmware versions, rack locations. The CMDB is boring until the outage — then it is everything.

example.code:
Firmware update day:
  1. Verify backups + maintenance window
  2. BMC first (keeps OOB access safe)
  3. BIOS/UEFI → reboot → verify
  4. RAID controller → verify array optimal
  5. Document versions; close the window.
  One component at a time, verified between each.
example.walkthrough: Treat firmware with the same discipline as OS patches: inventoried, scheduled, tested, documented. It is part of the attack surface.

pitfalls: 'Firmware doesn't get attacked' — BMC and UEFI implants are real and persistent.
No firmware inventory — you cannot patch what you cannot see.
Skipping secure decommission — disks outlive servers; erase or destroy.
lessons.try_it: Inventory the firmware versions of one system you manage. Any known CVEs? (Check vendor advisories.)

lessons.title: Hypervisor Sizing and Overcommit
concepts: Overcommit ratios are policy, not magic: CPU 4:1 is common, memory 1.2:1 is cautious (ballooning/swapping hurts), storage thin-provisioned with monitoring. Exceed them deliberately, not accidentally.
The real limits: CPU ready-time (<5%), memory ballooning (any sustained = pain), storage latency. Monitor the hypervisor's contention metrics, not just guest CPU%.
Right-size VMs first: oversized VMs waste the shared pool and inflate ready-time for everyone. Start small, grow on evidence — the opposite of physical servers.
NUMA awareness: keep VM memory within one NUMA node when possible; crossing nodes costs latency. Large VMs need NUMA planning, not just vCPU counts.
Plan host failure capacity: N+1 minimum — the cluster must absorb one host loss without contention. 'It fits when all hosts are up' is not HA.

example.code:
Cluster: 3 hosts × 20 cores, 256GB RAM.
  Usable (N+1): 40 cores, ~512GB RAM.
  VMs request: 60 vCPU, 400GB RAM.
  CPU overcommit 1.5:1 (fine), RAM 0.78:1 (fine).
  Ready-time 8% on host 2 → investigate noisy neighbor, not add hosts yet.
example.walkthrough: Virtualization is resource sharing with accounting: the hypervisor's contention metrics tell the truth that guest metrics hide. Read them.

pitfalls: Sizing VMs like physical servers — oversized guests tax the whole cluster.
Ignoring ready-time — the #1 hidden contention metric; guest CPU% lies by omission.
No N+1 capacity — the first host failure becomes a cascading performance event.
lessons.try_it: Calculate your cluster's N+1 usable capacity. Does current allocation fit? Show the math.

lessons.title: VM Templates and Golden Images
concepts: Golden images: build once, deploy many. Template = OS + patches + agents + hardening, sysprepped/generalized, versioned. Every VM starts identical and known.
Update the template monthly: patch, capture new version, deprecate old. VMs deployed from stale templates start life vulnerable — the template IS the baseline.
Customization specs (guest OS profiles): hostname, IP, domain join applied at deploy time. Template stays generic; identity comes from the spec.
Version and test: v2026.10 tested by deploying a canary VM and running smoke tests. Untested templates propagate brokenness at scale.
Immutable option: for cattle workloads, never patch running VMs — redeploy from the new template. Pets get patched; cattle get replaced.

example.code:
Template pipeline:
  1. Build VM from ISO → harden → install agents
  2. Sysprep/generalize → convert to template v2026.10
  3. Deploy canary → smoke tests pass
  4. Mark v2026.10 current; deprecate v2026.09
  5. All new VMs come from v2026.10 — automatically.
example.walkthrough: Templates turn server builds from craft projects into manufacturing: consistent, fast, auditable. The template version is a security control.

pitfalls: Snowflake VMs built by hand — unrepeatable, unauditable, unpatchable at scale.
Stale templates — 6-month-old images deploy 6 months of vulnerabilities.
No canary test — a broken template breaks every future deployment.
lessons.try_it: Document your golden image contents: OS, patches (as of date), agents, hardening. What is missing?

lessons.title: Snapshots: Powerful and Dangerous
concepts: Snapshots are change-block trackers, not backups: they record deltas for short-term rollback (patching, upgrades). They are not a backup strategy.
The danger: snapshots grow, merge slowly, and hurt performance. A snapshot chain 30 days old is a performance and space incident — commit or delete within 72 hours.
Snapshot etiquette: name with purpose + date + owner, set a reminder to remove, never snapshot production databases without app-aware quiescing (VSS).
Consolidation: deleting a snapshot merges deltas — on busy VMs this takes time and IOPS. Plan consolidations in windows, not during peak.
For real protection: snapshots for change control, proper backups (Veeam/agent) for recovery. Different tools, different jobs — never confuse them.

example.code:
Patch Tuesday done right:
  1. App-aware snapshot 'pre-patch-2026-10-14-js'
  2. Patch → verify app works
  3. Delete snapshot within 24h (verified good)
  Patch Tuesday done wrong:
  Snapshot from March still there, 400GB chain, VM crawling.
example.walkthrough: Snapshots are scalpels: precise, temporary, powerful. Left in, they become anchors. Date them, delete them.

pitfalls: Snapshots as backups — they live on the same storage; array failure kills both.
Month-old snapshot chains — performance death by a thousand deltas.
No app-aware quiescing for databases — crash-consistent snapshots may not restore cleanly.
lessons.try_it: Audit your snapshots now: list all, note ages. Any older than 72 hours? Commit or delete with a plan.

lessons.title: Backup Strategies That Survive Reality
concepts: 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 different media, 1 offsite. The offsite copy defeats fire/theft/ransomware; the second medium defeats correlated failures.
Full + incremental + differential: full weekly, incremental daily (small, fast), differential (grows through week). Restore = last full + all incrementals since — know the chain math.
RPO/RTO define the design: RPO (how much data can we lose) sets backup frequency; RTO (how fast must we restore) sets the restore architecture. Get both in writing from the business.
Test restores, not just backups: a backup that has never been restored is a hypothesis. Monthly test restores (files, then systems) are the program's proof.
Ransomware changes everything: immutable/offline copies are now mandatory, not nice-to-have. If ransomware can reach it, it is not a backup — it is a second copy waiting to be encrypted.

example.code:
Design for RPO 24h / RTO 4h:
  Nightly incremental to local NAS (fast restore)
  Weekly full to immutable cloud (ransomware-proof)
  Monthly restore test: random file + full VM
  Documented runbook; tested quarterly end-to-end.
  The RPO/RTO numbers chose every element.
example.walkthrough: Backups are measured at restore time. Design from the RTO backward: what must be running in 4 hours, and what does that require?

pitfalls: Untested backups — the #1 backup failure; test restores are the job.
No offline/immutable copy — ransomware encrypts reachable backups first.
RPO/RTO never defined — without targets, any backup 'works' until it doesn't.
lessons.try_it: Write the RPO/RTO for your most critical system (ask if you must). Does the current backup design meet them?

lessons.title: Storage Tiers and Lifecycle
concepts: Tier by access pattern: hot (SSD, milliseconds), warm (disk, seconds), cold (tape/cloud archive, hours). Data cools with age — the tiering should follow automatically.
Lifecycle policies automate the cooling: 30 days hot → 90 days warm → 1 year archive. Manual tiering does not happen; policies do.
Deduplication and compression multiply effective capacity: backups dedupe 10:1 typically; compression 2:1 on text. Enable both where the workload benefits.
Monitor the growth rate, not just the usage: 'at current growth, we fill in 8 months' triggers procurement; 'we are at 80%' triggers panic. Trends beat thresholds.
Chargeback/showback by department: when storage has a visible cost, hoarding stops. Free infinite storage gets treated as infinite — because it is.

example.code:
File server, 20TB, growing 2TB/year:
  Hot (active projects): 5TB SSD
  Warm (last year): 8TB disk, auto-tier at 90 days
  Cold (archive): 7TB cloud archive, auto-tier at 1 year
  Growth: 2TB/yr → procure at 14 months, not at full.
example.walkthrough: Storage management is lifecycle management: data has a temperature, and the infrastructure should match it automatically.

pitfalls: Everything on hot tier — paying SSD prices for 3-year-old files nobody opens.
No lifecycle policies — manual tiering is a policy that never executes.
Ignoring growth rate — capacity planning needs the derivative, not just the level.
lessons.try_it: Classify your data into hot/warm/cold with age thresholds. What would auto-tiering save?

lessons.title: Database Backup Specifics
concepts: Database backups differ from file backups: consistency matters. Use native tools (pg_dump, SQL Server backup, mysqldump) or app-aware agents — file copies of live DBs corrupt.
Full + differential + log backups (SQL Server model): point-in-time recovery needs the log chain unbroken. One missing log backup = recovery stops there.
Test the restore INTO a scratch instance regularly: backup validity, restore procedure, and application smoke tests. The restore test IS the backup test.
Encryption: backup files contain everything — encrypt at rest and in transit. An unencrypted backup tape is a database on a truck.
Retention meets compliance: financial data 7 years, healthcare 6+, but also test that old backups RESTORE — format and tool compatibility decay over years.

example.code:
SQL Server, RPO 1h:
  Full: nightly 2 AM
  Differential: every 6 hours
  Log: every 15 minutes
  Restore test: monthly to scratch, app smoke test
  Worst case loss: 15 min of transactions. Chain verified monthly.
example.walkthrough: Database recovery is a chain: full → differential → logs. Every link tested, or the chain is decorative.

pitfalls: File-copy 'backups' of live databases — inconsistent and unrestorable; use native tools.
Untested log chains — point-in-time recovery is a claim until tested.
Unencrypted backup media — the backup is the database; protect it equally.
lessons.try_it: Map your database's backup chain: full/diff/log schedule. When was the last restore test?

lessons.title: Patch Management at Scale
concepts: Inventory first: you cannot patch what you cannot see. Asset inventory + patch status dashboard is the foundation — automate both.
Ring deployment: canary (5%) → pilot (25%) → broad (70%) → complete. Each ring validates before the next expands. The ring that catches the bad patch saves the fleet.
Maintenance windows by criticality: servers monthly, workstations weekly, emergency out-of-band for exploited vulns. The window is scheduled; the emergency is the exception.
Measure compliance, not activity: '% of systems patched within SLA' is the metric. 'Patches deployed' counts effort; compliance counts results.
Reboot management: pending reboots are unpatched systems. Track and enforce reboot compliance — the patch is not done until the reboot is done.

example.code:
Patch Tuesday:
  Day 1-2: test group (IT dept, canaries)
  Day 3-7: pilot (25%, watch for issues)
  Day 8-14: broad deployment
  Day 15: compliance report — <95% triggers escalation
  Emergency: exploited CVE → out-of-band, same rings, faster.
example.walkthrough: Patching is a manufacturing process: rings, windows, verification, metrics. Industrialize it or drown in it.

pitfalls: Big-bang patching — one bad patch, entire fleet down; rings exist for this reason.
No reboot tracking — 'patched' without reboot is unpatched with extra steps.
Measuring deployments not compliance — 1000 patches deployed, 60% compliant = failing.
lessons.try_it: What is your current patch compliance %? If unknown, that is the first problem to fix.

lessons.title: Endpoint Protection Strategy
concepts: Defense in depth for endpoints: EDR (behavioral) + next-gen AV (signatures + ML) + application allowlisting for high-value targets + disk encryption everywhere.
EDR over AV: signatures catch knowns; behavioral EDR catches the fileless, the living-off-the-land, the novel. In 2026, EDR is the baseline, not the upgrade.
Application allowlisting (ThreatLocker-style) flips the model: deny-by-default, allow only approved. The strongest endpoint control — and the most operationally demanding.
USB/device control: block mass storage by default, allow by exception with encryption requirements. The found USB drive is still an attack vector.
Measure: mean time to detect (MTTD), mean time to respond (MTTR), and coverage % (agents healthy). What gets measured gets defended.

example.code:
Laptop stolen at airport:
  Disk encrypted (BitLocker) → data safe
  EDR shows no new activity → likely powered off
  Remote wipe issued; device marked lost
  No data breach notification needed — encryption did its job.
  The control worked because it was deployed BEFORE the incident.
example.walkthrough: Endpoints are the perimeter now: every laptop is an internet-facing device. Protect accordingly — EDR, encryption, allowlisting.

pitfalls: AV-only in 2026 — signature-only defense against behavioral attacks.
Unencrypted laptops — a stolen unencrypted laptop IS a data breach.
No MTTD/MTTR tracking — you cannot improve what you do not measure.
lessons.try_it: Check your endpoints: EDR coverage %, encryption %, last MTTD. Which metric is weakest?

lessons.title: Security Baselines and Hardening
concepts: Baselines (CIS Benchmarks, STIGs) are the starting point: proven secure configurations for OS, apps, network gear. Start from the benchmark, document deviations.
Harden in layers: remove/disable unused services, least-privilege accounts, secure protocols only (no Telnet/FTP/HTTP-basic), logging enabled, patches current.
Group Policy / MDM / Ansible enforces the baseline continuously: drift happens (admins 'temporarily' change things); enforcement corrects it. Baseline without enforcement decays.
Audit against the baseline regularly: automated compliance scans (OpenSCAP, CIS-CAT) with trending. 'Compliant' is a point-in-time claim — trending proves the program.
Exceptions are managed, not ignored: business need documented, compensating controls defined, expiry dated, owner named. The exception process IS the security culture.

example.code:
New server build:
  1. Deploy from hardened image (CIS L1)
  2. Join to config management (enforcement)
  3. Scan: 94% compliant — 3 exceptions documented
  4. Schedule: monthly rescan, trending dashboard
  The server is born secure and stays that way — by process.
example.walkthrough: Hardening is not a project; it is a lifecycle: baseline → enforce → audit → remediate, forever. The loop is the control.

pitfalls: Manual hardening per server — snowflakes that drift; automate from images.
No exception expiry — 'temporary' exceptions become permanent vulnerabilities.
Audit once, never again — compliance decays; trending is the proof of program health.
lessons.try_it: Run a CIS benchmark scan (or review one) for a system you manage. What is the compliance %? Top 3 findings?

lessons.title: PBQ Command-Line Speed Runs
concepts: PBQs award partial credit per checkpoint: every verified fix (service restarted, port listening, config corrected) scores even if you don't finish the whole scenario, so front-load the easy checkpoints.

The 10-minute triage loop: status -> logs -> ports -> config. `systemctl status`, `journalctl -xe`, `ss -tlnp`, then read the config the log points at. Never start editing before the log tells you what's wrong.

Budget PBQs at 8-12 minutes each: set a mental timer, and when it rings, bank your checkpoints and move on — one perfect PBQ is worth less than one good PBQ plus six answered multiple-choice questions.
Read the PBQ task text twice before touching the terminal: half of PBQ failures come from fixing the wrong thing fast instead of the right thing deliberately.

example.code:
systemctl status nginx  # is it running?
journalctl -u nginx -n 20  # why did it fail?
ss -tlnp | grep 443       # is anything listening?
nginx -t                  # is the config valid?
example.walkthrough: This four-command sequence answers the four questions that solve 80% of service PBQs: state, cause, network, config. Each command's output tells you whether to go deeper or move to the next check — you never guess, and you never edit blind.

pitfalls: Pitfall: editing configs before reading logs — you create a second problem on top of the first and lose the trail.
Pitfall: rebooting the VM 'to fix it' — reboots destroy log evidence, take minutes, and rarely fix config errors.
Pitfall: perfectionism — spending 25 minutes polishing one PBQ while 15 multiple-choice questions go unanswered.
lessons.try_it: Spin up any Linux VM, break nginx three different ways (bad port, bad config syntax, stopped service), and time yourself diagnosing each with only the four-command sequence — aim for under 3 minutes per break.

lessons.title: Scenario Stem Parsing Under Pressure
concepts: Read the last sentence first: it defines the decision. Everything before it is either a constraint that discriminates between choices or a distractor.
Constraints are numbers and requirements (RTO 2h, 100 Mbps WAN, 50 switches, HIPAA) — circle them mentally and eliminate any choice that violates one.
Distractors are impressive-but-irrelevant details (company history, brand names, exact headcount when the question is technical) — notice them, then ignore them.
For BEST/MOST questions, the tiebreaker is always scale: which choice's advantage grows with the numbers in the stem?

example.code:
Stem: 'Hospital, HIPAA, RTO 2h, 100 Mbps WAN, 8TB data.'
Q: 'Which backup architecture meets the RTO?'
-> HIPAA = encryption constraint (not architecture)
-> 8TB / 100Mbps = ~7.4 days for off-site full restore >> 2h RTO
-> Eliminate anything requiring off-site full restores.
example.walkthrough: The last sentence asks about RTO, so the discriminating constraint is the math: 8TB over 100 Mbps cannot restore in 2 hours. HIPAA matters for encryption-in-transit, not for the architecture choice. One calculation eliminates two choices instantly.

pitfalls: Pitfall: keyword matching — picking the choice that repeats a stem buzzword (like HIPAA) instead of the one that satisfies the actual question.
Pitfall: re-reading the whole stem three times — if you're stuck, you've missed the constraint; re-read only the last sentence and the numbers.
Pitfall: choosing the most advanced technology — exams test appropriateness, not impressiveness.
lessons.try_it: Take 5 practice scenario questions, cover the choices, and write down in one line what the last sentence asks plus the discriminating numbers — then uncover and eliminate. Track how often the elimination alone picks the answer.

lessons.title: Right-Sizing VM Resources
concepts: Size on p95 utilization, not averages: averages hide the peaks that cause outages, while p95 captures real demand plus natural headroom.
Separate steady from spiky workloads: steady VMs get fixed sizes near p95, spiky ones get burstable classes or autoscaling so you pay for peaks only when they happen.
Memory and CPU size independently: most fleets are CPU-idle but memory-heavy (or vice versa) — right-size each dimension on its own p95.
Stage every resize with rollback: change one workload group at a time, watch for a full business cycle, and keep the revert command ready — evidence beats arguments with nervous engineering teams.

example.code:
# Per-VM p95 over 30 days (example via cloud metrics CLI)
# vm-web-04: p95 CPU 22% of 8 vCPU -> target 4 vCPU (p95 ~44%)
# vm-web-04: p95 mem 61% of 32GB  -> target 16GB (p95 ~75%)
# Rollback: snapshot the sizing change; revert = one API call
example.walkthrough: The p95 math turns 'feels over-provisioned' into a defensible target: halving vCPU still leaves the p95 at 44%, well clear of saturation. Doing it per workload group with a one-command revert is what gets the change approved.

pitfalls: Pitfall: sizing on averages — a VM averaging 20% CPU with 95% spikes will fall over the first time you halve it.
Pitfall: resizing everything at once — one bad assumption becomes a fleet-wide incident with no clean rollback.
Pitfall: ignoring memory — CPU-rightsized VMs that OOM are worse than the waste you started with.
lessons.try_it: Pull 30 days of CPU/memory metrics for 5 VMs you own, compute p95 for each, and propose new sizes with the headroom math written out — then check whether any p95 would exceed 70% after the change.

lessons.title: Hybrid Workload Placement Matrix
concepts: Place by workload shape: steady-state systems (ERP, scheduling, core banking) gain nothing from elasticity and stay where controls exist; spiky systems (analytics, rendering, seasonal web) pay for idle capacity on-prem and belong in cloud.

Data sensitivity is a placement input, not a veto: PHI/financial data can live in cloud with the right controls, but audit and residency requirements may still anchor it on-prem — evaluate, don't assume.
Data gravity decides ties: the 40TB dataset's location dictates where its compute runs, because moving terabytes nightly is a permanent tax.
Revisit placement yearly: workload shapes change (that 'spiky' pipeline becomes 24/7), and last year's right answer rots into this year's waste.

example.code:
Workload            | Shape    | Data        | Placement
--------------------|----------|-------------|------------------
Patient scheduling  | steady   | PHI, audit  | on-prem
Research analytics  | 6h/week  | de-identified| cloud (spot GPUs)
Claims archive      | cold     | regulated   | cloud archive tier
CI runners          | spiky    | code        | cloud autoscale
example.walkthrough: Each row scores shape against sensitivity: the steady PHI system stays where the audit controls are, the spiky GPU job rents instead of buying 200 idle GPUs, cold regulated data gets cheap archive storage, and spiky CI scales to zero. No absolutism — every placement earns its row.

pitfalls: Pitfall: 'cloud-first' or 'on-prem-first' as policy — blanket rules optimize one workload shape at every other shape's expense.
Pitfall: placing compute far from its data — the nightly terabyte transfer becomes a permanent cost and SLA risk.
Pitfall: set-and-forget placement — a workload that goes from batch to real-time needs re-placement, not nostalgia.
lessons.try_it: List 6 workloads you know, score each on shape (steady/spiky), data sensitivity, and data gravity, and place each — then find one placement from last year that the scores say should move.

lessons.title: Idempotent Infrastructure Scripts
concepts: Idempotent means re-runnable: running the script twice produces the same end state as running it once — this is what makes automation safe to retry after partial failures.
The pattern is check-then-converge: every action first reads current state (does the VM exist? is the disk attached? is the package installed?) and only acts on the gap.
Desired-state tools (Terraform, Ansible) are idempotent by design; imperative scripts must earn it — a bash script that blindly runs `useradd` twice is a bug, not automation.
Test idempotency explicitly: run the script, run it again, and diff the world — the second run should report zero changes.

example.code:
# Non-idempotent: creates dupes on retry
aws ec2 run-instances --count 1 ...

# Idempotent: converge toward desired state
if ! vm_exists "web-04"; then
  aws ec2 run-instances --tag Name=web-04 ...
fi
# Better: let Terraform/Ansible own the state check
example.walkthrough: The first version creates a second VM every retry — the exact failure mode that teaches teams to fear re-running automation. The guarded version checks existence first, so retries converge instead of duplicating. The lesson: retries are normal, so scripts must survive them.

pitfalls: Pitfall: 'run once' assumptions — every script will eventually be re-run after a partial failure; design for it on day one.
Pitfall: checking the wrong state — verifying the VM exists but not that the disk attached still duplicates disks.
Pitfall: manual cleanup runbooks as the idempotency strategy — they institutionalize fragility instead of fixing it.
lessons.try_it: Take any deploy script you own, run it twice against a test environment, and list every duplicate or error the second run creates — then add existence checks until the second run is a clean no-op.

lessons.title: High-Availability Architecture Patterns
concepts: Design for failure domains: spread across availability zones for rack/power/network failures, and across regions only when the business cost of a regional outage justifies the complexity.

Stateless tiers scale horizontally behind load balancers; stateful tiers need explicit strategies — replication with automated failover for databases, shared/distributed storage for files, externalized sessions for app servers.
Active-passive is simpler and cheaper but fails over slowly (DNS, promotion lag); active-active is seamless but demands conflict resolution — pick by RTO, not by fashion.
Health checks are the nervous system: load balancers, auto-scalers, and failover all depend on accurate health signals — a bad health check turns a single failure into a cascading one.

example.code:
# Classic 3-tier HA sketch
# Tier 1: ALB across 3 AZs, health-checked, auto-scaling 3-30
# Tier 2: app servers stateless, sessions in ElastiCache
# Tier 3: RDS Multi-AZ (sync standby), read replicas for scale
# DNS: Route53 health-checked failover to passive region
example.walkthrough: Every tier has its own HA story matched to its statefulness: the stateless web tier just scales, sessions move to a shared store so any server can serve any user, the database uses synchronous standby for failover, and DNS provides the regional escape hatch. No tier depends on a single box.

pitfalls: Pitfall: single-AZ databases with 'we'll restore from backup' — restores take hours; Multi-AZ failover takes minutes.
Pitfall: sticky sessions as a substitute for shared session state — they break the moment auto-scaling replaces an instance.
Pitfall: health checks that always return 200 — the load balancer keeps sending traffic to a dead app.
lessons.try_it: Draw your most important service's architecture, mark every single point of failure (single AZ, single instance, local sessions), and write the one-line fix for each — then rank the fixes by outage cost avoided.

lessons.title: systemd Troubleshooting Playbook
concepts: Units are the model: services, sockets, timers, and mounts are all units with states (active, failed, inactive) — `systemctl status` is always step one.
The journal is the memory: `journalctl -u <service>` shows that unit's logs, `-xe` adds explanations, `--since '10 min ago'` bounds the search — most 'mystery' failures confess here.
Dependencies are the map: `systemctl list-dependencies` and the After=/Requires= directives explain ordering failures — a service that 'randomly' fails at boot usually starts before its dependency.
Overrides beat edits: never modify vendor unit files in /usr/lib — use `systemctl edit` to create drop-ins in /etc, so updates don't wipe your changes.

example.code:
systemctl status app.service        # state + recent log tail
journalctl -u app.service -n 50   # the failure story
systemctl list-dependencies app.service  # what must start first
systemctl edit app.service        # safe override drop-in
systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart app.service
example.walkthrough: This is the complete loop: observe state, read the story, check ordering, fix safely via drop-in, reload, restart. Following it in order means you never edit a unit file that an update will overwrite, and you never restart before understanding the failure.

pitfalls: Pitfall: editing /usr/lib/systemd unit files directly — the next package update silently reverts your fix.
Pitfall: `systemctl restart` as the first step — it destroys the failed state that would have told you the cause.
Pitfall: forgetting daemon-reload after unit changes — systemd keeps running the old definition and your fix 'doesn't work'.
lessons.try_it: Break a test service three ways (bad ExecStart path, missing After= dependency, wrong permissions), and recover each using only status, journalctl, list-dependencies, and edit — no reinstalling.

simulations.title: The disk that filled up
simulations.brief: A VM stops accepting writes: the app logs 'No space left on device', but the dashboard shows the disk at 57%.

steps.symptom: Writes fail with 'No space left', yet the volume shows 57% used.
evidence:
$ df
/dev/sda1  57% /
$ echo test > /tmp/t
bash: /tmp/t: No space left on device
options: Suspect inode exhaustion: check inode usage — a full inode table blocks new files with space to spare
steps.explain: 'No space left' with free blocks means inodes, not bytes: millions of tiny files (often runaway logs or sessions) exhausted the inode table.

steps.symptom: Confirmed: inode table at 100% on /tmp — millions of session files.
options: Clear the stale session files and fix the app to clean up sessions (tmpwatch/cron)
steps.explain: Clear the symptom (stale files) AND the cause (no session cleanup). Disk expansion wouldn't help — inodes, not bytes, were exhausted.

steps.symptom: Cleanup done. Verify the fix holds.
evidence:
$ df -i
/dev/sda1  12% /
$ echo test > /tmp/t && echo OK
OK
options: Confirm writes succeed and inode usage is healthy, and the cleanup job is scheduled
steps.explain: Writes succeeding plus healthy inodes plus a scheduled cleanup is the complete fix — one without the others recurs.

simulations.debrief: 'No space left' with free space means inodes. Clear the files, fix the leak (session cleanup), schedule the prevention. df without -i only tells half the story.

simulations.brief: Restore the order of the virtualization stack from silicon to app.

items: Physical hardware: CPU, RAM, disk

simulations.title: Scale up or scale out?
simulations.brief: Choose the scaling strategy for two workloads.

steps.text: A stateful database is slow. It holds 2 TB and can't easily shard. Strategy?

choices.label: Scale up: bigger instance — stateful stores with hard sharding limits scale vertically first
choices.feedback: Right: when the data can't split, grow the box. Sharding a 2 TB store under load is a migration, not a scaling event.

choices.label: Scale out: add 10 replicas
choices.feedback: Replicas of a write-heavy unshardable store multiply the consistency problem, not the capacity.

choices.label: Delete old data
choices.feedback: Deleting production data to fix performance is data loss with extra steps.

steps.text: A stateless API tier is slow at peak. Strategy?

choices.label: Scale out: add instances behind the load balancer — stateless tiers scale horizontally
choices.feedback: Right: stateless means any instance can serve any request — add more of them.

choices.label: Scale up: one giant instance
choices.feedback: One giant instance is a single point of failure with a scaling ceiling.

simulations.debrief: Stateful and hard-to-shard → scale up. Stateless → scale out. The workload's statefulness decides, not the cloud bill.

simulations.title: The backup that never ran
simulations.brief: Backups report 'success' but restores find nothing. The backup config has 2 bugs in 8 lines.

steps.config:
schedule: daily 02:00
source: /data
target: /mnt/backup
retention: 7
verify: false
notify: never
# last restore test: never
# owner: infra-team

issues.description: verify: false — backups are never validated, so silent corruption or empty runs report success.
issues.fix: Enable verification (checksums/test restores) on every run.

issues.description: No restore has ever been tested — an untested backup is a hope, not a recovery plan.
issues.fix: Run scheduled restore drills and record the results.

simulations.debrief: Backups are only real if they're verified and restores are tested. 'Success' without verification is a green lie.

sections.heading: Cloud Architecture
items: Shared responsibility splits at the hypervisor for IaaS — the provider secures facilities, hardware, and virtualization; you own the OS, middleware, apps, and data.
